skeletal.name: Skeletal
skeletal.desc: 206 bones — support, protection, movement, mineral storage, hematopoiesis.

structures.name: Skull (Cranium)
structures.fn: Protects the brain. 22 bones form the cranial vault (frontal, parietal×2, temporal×2, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid) and facial skeleton (14 bones).
structures.clinical: Fractures may cause epidural or subdural hematoma. Open fontanelles in infants allow brain growth and molding during birth.
structures.clinicalKid: Your skull is a strong helmet of bone that wraps around your brain and keeps it safe. It is made of many bones that grow together as you get bigger. Wearing a helmet when you bike or skate helps protect your skull, and a doctor can check it to make sure it is healthy.
structures.detail: Houses meninges, brain, and cranial nerve foramina. Fontanelles close during infancy and early childhood; major cranial sutures normally remain into adulthood and fuse much later, if at all.

structures.name: Mandible
structures.fn: Only moveable skull bone. Enables mastication, speech, and facial expression. Houses lower teeth.
structures.clinical: TMJ dysfunction causes jaw pain and clicking. Mandibular fractures are the second most common facial fracture.

structures.name: Clavicle
structures.fn: Horizontal strut connecting scapula to sternum. Transmits forces from upper limb to axial skeleton.
structures.clinical: Most frequently fractured bone (fall on outstretched hand). Middle third fractures most common.

structures.name: Sternum
structures.fn: Flat bone protecting heart and great vessels. Manubrium, body, and xiphoid process. Site for bone marrow biopsy in adults.
structures.clinical: Sternal fractures from blunt chest trauma (steering wheel). CPR may cause xiphoid fractures.

structures.name: Ribs (1-12)
structures.fn: 12 pairs: 7 true (1–7), 3 false (8–10), 2 floating (11–12). Protect thoracic organs and assist ventilation.
structures.clinical: Flail chest: 3+ adjacent ribs fractured in 2+ places. Rib fractures 9–11 may lacerate spleen or liver.
structures.clinicalKid: Your ribs are curved bones that make a strong cage around your chest to keep your heart and lungs safe. They also move a little to help you breathe in and out. Drinking milk, eating healthy food, and staying active help your bones grow strong.

structures.name: Scapula
structures.fn: Triangular flat bone on posterior thorax. Attachment for 17 muscles. Acromion and coracoid processes are key landmarks.
structures.clinical: Winged scapula from long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) palsy — serratus anterior paralysis.

structures.name: Humerus
structures.fn: Upper arm bone. Articulates with scapula (shoulder) and radius/ulna (elbow). Greater/lesser tubercles for rotator cuff.
structures.clinical: Midshaft fracture → radial nerve palsy (wrist drop). Surgical neck fracture → axillary nerve injury.
structures.clinicalKid: Your humerus is the long bone in your upper arm that connects your shoulder to your elbow. It helps you reach, throw, and lift things every day. Drinking milk, eating healthy food, and staying active help your bones grow strong, and a doctor can check them with an X-ray.

structures.name: Radius
structures.fn: Lateral forearm bone. Pivots around ulna for pronation/supination. Radial head at elbow, styloid process at wrist.
structures.clinical: Colles fracture: distal radius fracture from FOOSH (fall on outstretched hand). "Dinner fork" deformity.

structures.name: Ulna
structures.fn: Medial forearm bone. Olecranon forms elbow point. Trochlear notch articulates with humerus for hinge motion.
structures.clinical: Olecranon fractures from direct trauma. Monteggia fracture: proximal ulna + radial head dislocation.

structures.name: Carpals
structures.fn: 8 small bones in 2 rows: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform (proximal); trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate (distal).
structures.clinical: Scaphoid fracture: anatomical snuffbox tenderness. Avascular necrosis risk due to retrograde blood supply.

structures.name: Vertebral Column
structures.fn: 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral (fused), 4 coccygeal (fused). Protects spinal cord. Four curves provide spring-like shock absorption.
structures.clinical: Herniated disc (L4–L5, L5–S1 most common). Scoliosis, kyphosis, lordosis. Spinal stenosis.
structures.clinicalKid: Your spine is a stack of small bones that holds you up straight and lets you bend and twist. Its gentle curves work like a spring so it can soak up bumps when you run and jump, and it keeps the bundle of nerves inside it safe. Sitting up tall, staying active, and lifting heavy things with care help keep it strong.

structures.name: Pelvis
structures.fn: Ilium, ischium, pubis fused at acetabulum. Transfers weight from spine to lower limbs. Male pelvis narrower; female pelvis wider for childbirth.
structures.clinical: Pelvic fractures → life-threatening hemorrhage from internal iliac vessels. Acetabular fractures require surgical fixation.
structures.clinicalKid: Your pelvis is a strong bowl of bones at the bottom of your spine that holds your body up and connects to your legs. It helps you stand, walk, run, and sit down. Eating healthy foods and staying active help keep your bones strong.

structures.name: Femur
structures.fn: Longest, strongest bone. Head fits into acetabulum. Neck angled 125°. Supports 2–3× body weight during walking.
structures.clinical: Hip fractures in elderly have 20–30% one-year mortality. Femoral neck fractures may disrupt blood supply → avascular necrosis.
structures.clinicalKid: Your femur is the longest and strongest bone in your body, and it sits in your thigh between your hip and your knee. It is so strong that it can hold up your whole body when you walk, run, and jump. Drinking milk, eating healthy food, and playing outside help keep your bones strong.

structures.name: Patella
structures.fn: Largest sesamoid bone. Embedded in quadriceps tendon. Increases mechanical advantage of quadriceps by 30%.
structures.clinical: Patellar fracture from direct trauma or forceful quad contraction. Patellofemoral syndrome ("runner's knee").

structures.name: Tibia
structures.fn: Main weight-bearing bone of the leg. Medial malleolus forms inner ankle. Tibial plateau articulates with femoral condyles.
structures.clinical: Tibial plateau fractures from axial loading. Open fractures common (subcutaneous anterior surface). Compartment syndrome risk.

structures.name: Fibula
structures.fn: Non-weight-bearing lateral leg bone. Lateral malleolus forms outer ankle. Attachment for interosseous membrane and lateral compartment muscles.
structures.clinical: Lateral malleolus fractures in ankle sprains. Maisonneuve fracture: proximal fibula + medial ankle injury.

structures.name: Tarsals
structures.fn: 7 bones: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, 3 cuneiforms. Form longitudinal and transverse foot arches for shock absorption.
structures.clinical: Calcaneal fractures from axial loading (falls from height). Talus fractures risk avascular necrosis.

structures.name: Sacrum & Coccyx
structures.fn: Sacrum: 5 fused vertebrae forming posterior pelvis. Sacral canal contains cauda equina. Coccyx: vestigial tail bone.
structures.clinical: Sacral fractures in high-energy trauma. Coccydynia (tailbone pain) from falls or prolonged sitting.

structures.name: Hyoid Bone
structures.fn: U-shaped bone at C3 level. Only bone not articulating with another bone — suspended by muscles and ligaments. Anchors tongue and aids swallowing and speech. Greater and lesser horns (cornua).
structures.clinical: Hyoid fracture strongly associated with strangulation (forensic significance). Important in swallowing disorders (dysphagia evaluation). Attachment for suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles.

structures.name: Atlas (C1) & Axis (C2)
structures.fn: Atlas (C1): ring-shaped, no body or spinous process. Supports skull, allows nodding (yes). Axis (C2): has odontoid process (dens) that acts as pivot. Atlas rotates around dens for head rotation (no). Transverse ligament holds dens against atlas.
structures.clinical: Jefferson fracture (C1 burst from axial loading). Hangman fracture (C2 pedicle bilateral fracture). Atlantoaxial subluxation in rheumatoid arthritis and Down syndrome. Odontoid fractures in elderly falls.

structures.name: Metatarsals & Phalanges (Foot)
structures.fn: 5 metatarsals form forefoot, 14 phalanges (great toe has 2, others have 3). First metatarsal bears most weight during push-off. Metatarsal heads form "ball of foot." Sesamoid bones under 1st metatarsal head.
structures.clinical: Jones fracture (5th metatarsal base): poor healing due to watershed blood supply. Stress fractures in runners (2nd/3rd metatarsal). Morton neuroma: interdigital nerve compression. Hallux valgus (bunion).

structures.name: Metacarpals & Phalanges (Hand)
structures.fn: 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges. Thumb (1st metacarpal) has saddle joint at CMC for opposition — unique to primates. Each finger has 3 phalanges (proximal, middle, distal) except thumb (2). Extensor mechanism on dorsum.
structures.clinical: Boxer fracture (5th metacarpal neck). Bennett fracture (1st metacarpal base). Mallet finger (extensor tendon avulsion at DIP). Jersey finger (FDP avulsion). Dupuytren contracture: palmar fascia thickening.

structures.name: Scaphoid Bone
structures.fn: Largest carpal bone in proximal row. Crosses both carpal rows, making it vulnerable to fracture. Blood supply enters distally (retrograde) — fractures may disrupt blood flow to proximal pole. Palpable in anatomical snuffbox.
structures.clinical: Most commonly fractured carpal bone (FOOSH mechanism). Anatomical snuffbox tenderness is key exam finding. Risk of avascular necrosis of proximal pole (retrograde blood supply). Often missed on initial X-ray — requires repeat imaging or MRI.

muscular.name: Muscular
muscular.desc: 600+ muscles — movement, posture, heat production, joint stabilization.

structures.name: Deltoid
structures.fn: Primary shoulder abductor (middle fibers). Anterior fibers flex/medially rotate; posterior fibers extend/laterally rotate the arm.
structures.origin: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, scapular spine
structures.clinical: Atrophy from axillary nerve injury (C5–C6). IM injection site (avoid in children < 3 yrs).
structures.clinicalKid: Your deltoid is the rounded muscle that caps the top of your shoulder and helps you lift your arm up and out to the side. Playing, swimming, and reaching for things keep it strong. This is also a spot where doctors sometimes give you a shot.

structures.name: Pectoralis Major
structures.fn: Powerful arm adductor, flexor, and medial rotator. Clavicular head flexes; sternocostal head adducts and extends from flexed position.
structures.origin: Clavicle, sternum, ribs 1–6, external oblique aponeurosis
structures.clinical: Rupture during bench press — "dropped pec" sign. Poland syndrome: congenital absence.

structures.name: Biceps Brachii
structures.fn: Powerful forearm supinator and elbow flexor. Long head stabilizes shoulder joint. Short head assists shoulder flexion.
structures.origin: Short head: coracoid process; Long head: supraglenoid tubercle
structures.clinical: Long head tendon rupture → "Popeye deformity." Biceps reflex tests C5–C6 nerve roots.
structures.clinicalKid: Your biceps is the muscle in the front of your upper arm that bends your elbow so you can lift and carry things, and it helps you turn your wrist too. Moving, climbing, and playing keep it strong. Eating good food and resting after hard play help it grow.

structures.name: Triceps Brachii
structures.fn: Only elbow extensor. Three heads: long (crosses shoulder), lateral, and medial. Essential for pushing movements.
structures.origin: Long: infraglenoid tubercle; Lateral/medial: posterior humerus
structures.clinical: Weakness in radial nerve palsy (C7 root). Triceps reflex tests C7–C8 nerve roots.

structures.name: Rectus Abdominis
structures.fn: Flexes trunk (sit-ups/crunches). Compresses abdominal contents. Assists forced expiration and stabilizes pelvis during walking.
structures.origin: Pubic crest and symphysis
structures.clinical: Diastasis recti: midline separation (common in pregnancy). "Six-pack" — tendinous intersections create segmented appearance.

structures.name: External Obliques
structures.fn: Trunk rotation (contralateral), lateral flexion, and abdominal compression. Largest and most superficial abdominal muscle.
structures.origin: External surfaces of ribs 5–12
structures.insertion: Linea alba, pubic tubercle, iliac crest
structures.clinical: Strains from twisting sports. Inguinal ligament (lower border) is key landmark for hernia surgery.

structures.name: Quadriceps Femoris
structures.fn: Four muscles (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis/medialis/intermedius). Primary knee extensor. Rectus femoris also flexes hip.
structures.origin: Rectus femoris: AIIS; Vasti: femoral shaft
structures.clinical: Quadriceps tendon/patellar tendon rupture. VMO weakness → patellofemoral tracking issues.
structures.clinicalKid: Your quadriceps are four strong muscles on the front of your thigh that straighten your knee and help lift your leg. They power you when you run, jump, climb stairs, and stand up. Moving your body, stretching, and resting your legs keep them strong.

structures.name: Hamstrings
structures.fn: Three muscles (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus). Flex knee and extend hip. Critical for deceleration in running.
structures.origin: Ischial tuberosity (all three); biceps femoris short head: linea aspera
structures.insertion: Biceps: fibular head; Semi-T: pes anserinus; Semi-M: posterior medial tibial condyle
structures.clinical: "Pulled hamstring" — most common muscle strain in athletes. Proximal avulsion in sprinters.
structures.clinicalKid: Your hamstrings are the strong muscles on the back of your legs that help you bend your knees and run, jump, and slow down. Warming up before you play and stretching gently keep them loose and healthy. Drinking water and resting after exercise help them feel good too.

structures.name: Gastrocnemius
structures.fn: Superficial calf muscle. Powerful plantar flexor (push-off in gait) and weak knee flexor. Two heads span the knee joint.
structures.origin: Medial and lateral femoral condyles
structures.clinical: Achilles tendon rupture (positive Thompson test). "Tennis leg" — medial head tear.
structures.clinicalKid: Your gastrocnemius is the big calf muscle on the back of your lower leg, and it helps you push off the ground when you walk, run, and jump. It also lets you stand up on your tiptoes. Moving around, stretching, and warming up before you play keep it strong and ready.

structures.name: Trapezius
structures.fn: Large diamond-shaped muscle. Upper fibers elevate scapula (shrug); middle fibers retract; lower fibers depress and rotate scapula upward.
structures.origin: External occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, C7–T12 spinous processes
structures.insertion: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, scapular spine
structures.clinical: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) palsy → inability to shrug shoulder. Shoulder droop.

structures.name: Latissimus Dorsi
structures.fn: Broadest back muscle. Powerful arm extensor, adductor, and medial rotator. Key muscle in swimming, climbing, and pull-ups.
structures.origin: T6–T12 spinous processes, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, ribs 9–12
structures.clinical: Used in reconstructive surgery (myocutaneous flaps). Thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8) innervation.

structures.name: Gluteus Maximus
structures.fn: Largest muscle in the body. Powerful hip extensor and lateral rotator. Essential for standing from seated position, climbing stairs, running.
structures.origin: Posterior ilium, sacrum, coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament
structures.insertion: IT band and gluteal tuberosity of femur
structures.clinical: Weakness → Trendelenburg gait (compensatory trunk lean). Inferior gluteal nerve (L5–S2).

structures.name: Sartorius
structures.fn: Longest muscle in the body. Crosses hip and knee. Produces the "tailor's position" (cross-legged sitting): hip flexion, abduction, lateral rotation + knee flexion.
structures.origin: Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)
structures.clinical: Pes anserinus bursitis causes medial knee pain. Landmark for femoral triangle.

structures.name: Tibialis Anterior
structures.fn: Primary ankle dorsiflexor and foot inverter. Prevents foot slap during heel strike. Supports medial longitudinal arch.
structures.origin: Lateral tibial condyle, upper 2/3 of lateral tibial surface
structures.clinical: Foot drop from deep peroneal nerve injury. Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome).

structures.name: Soleus
structures.fn: Deep calf muscle beneath gastrocnemius. Plantar flexion (postural muscle — prevents forward falling while standing). Does not cross knee.
structures.origin: Soleal line and posterior proximal fibula
structures.clinical: Soleus muscle pump aids venous return. DVT risk when immobile (long flights). Soleus strain in runners.

structures.name: Rotator Cuff (SITS)
structures.fn: Four muscles: Supraspinatus (initiates abduction, most commonly torn), Infraspinatus (lateral rotation), Teres minor (lateral rotation), Subscapularis (medial rotation). Stabilize glenohumeral joint and keep humeral head in glenoid fossa.
structures.origin: Scapula (various fossae)
structures.insertion: Greater and lesser tubercles of humerus
structures.clinical: Rotator cuff tears: most common shoulder pathology (especially supraspinatus). Impingement syndrome: supraspinatus compressed under acromion during abduction. Positive empty can test, drop arm test.

structures.name: Iliopsoas
structures.fn: Compound muscle: iliacus + psoas major. Most powerful hip flexor. Psoas major originates from T12–L5 vertebral bodies (only muscle connecting spine to lower limb). Critical for walking, running, and maintaining upright posture.
structures.origin: Psoas: T12–L5 vertebrae. Iliacus: iliac fossa
structures.clinical: Psoas abscess from spinal TB or Crohn disease. Psoas sign: pain on hip extension (suggests appendicitis/abscess). Hip flexion contracture in elderly/wheelchair-bound. Thomas test for hip flexion contracture.

structures.name: Intercostal Muscles
structures.fn: Three layers between ribs. External intercostals: elevate ribs for inspiration. Internal intercostals: depress ribs for forced expiration. Innermost intercostals: similar to internal. Intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in costal groove (vein, artery, nerve — VAN, superior to inferior).
structures.origin: Inferior border of rib above
structures.clinical: Intercostal nerve block for rib fracture pain. Chest tube insertion above rib to avoid neurovascular bundle. Intercostal neuralgia: chronic chest wall pain. Herpes zoster (shingles) follows intercostal dermatome.

structures.name: Pelvic Floor (Levator Ani)
structures.fn: Muscular "hammock" supporting pelvic organs: pubococcygeus, puborectalis, iliococcygeus. Supports bladder, uterus/prostate, rectum. Puborectalis maintains fecal continence (anorectal angle). Contracts during Kegel exercises.
structures.origin: Pubis, obturator fascia (arcus tendineus), ischial spine
structures.clinical: Pelvic floor weakness: urinary incontinence, pelvic organ prolapse (cystocele, rectocele, uterine prolapse). Common after vaginal delivery. Kegel exercises for strengthening. Pelvic floor dysfunction: chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia.

structures.name: Diaphragm (Muscle)
structures.fn: Primary muscle of respiration (responsible for 70% of quiet breathing). Dome-shaped musculotendinous partition between thorax and abdomen. Central tendon + peripheral muscle fibers from xiphoid, ribs 7–12, L1–L3 vertebrae (crura). Right crus larger, encircles esophagus.
structures.origin: Xiphoid process, costal cartilages 7–12, L1–L3 crura
structures.clinical: Hiccups: involuntary diaphragm spasm. Phrenic nerve (C3–C5): "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive." Diaphragmatic hernia: abdominal contents in thorax. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek): left-sided, neonatal respiratory distress.

circulatory.name: Circulatory
circulatory.desc: Heart, 60,000 miles of vessels, 5L of blood — delivers O₂, nutrients, hormones; removes waste.

structures.name: Heart
structures.fn: Muscular pump. 4 chambers: RA/RV (pulmonary circuit), LA/LV (systemic circuit). Beats ~100,000×/day, pumps ~5L/min at rest.
structures.clinical: MI (heart attack): coronary artery occlusion. Heart failure, arrhythmias, valvular disease. Leading cause of death worldwide.
structures.clinicalKid: Your heart is a strong muscle about the size of your fist that pumps blood all day and night. Running, playing, and eating fruits and vegetables keep it strong. A doctor can listen to it beat with a stethoscope.

structures.name: Aorta
structures.fn: Largest artery. Ascending aorta → aortic arch (brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian) → descending thoracic → abdominal aorta.
structures.clinical: Aortic aneurysm (abdominal > 5.5cm → surgical repair). Aortic dissection: tearing chest pain, emergency.
structures.clinicalKid: Your aorta is the biggest blood tube in your body, and it carries fresh blood away from your heart to the rest of you. It starts at the heart, makes a big curve at the top, and then heads down to send blood to your belly and legs. Running, playing, and eating fruits and vegetables help keep it strong and healthy.

structures.name: Superior Vena Cava
structures.fn: Returns deoxygenated blood from head, neck, upper limbs, and thorax to the right atrium. Formed by union of brachiocephalic veins.
structures.clinical: SVC syndrome: obstruction (often by lung cancer/lymphoma) causes facial swelling, dyspnea, distended neck veins.

structures.name: Inferior Vena Cava
structures.fn: Largest vein. Returns blood from lower body to right atrium. Formed at L5 by union of common iliac veins. Passes through diaphragm at T8.
structures.clinical: IVC filter placement for recurrent PE. IVC compression during pregnancy (supine hypotension syndrome).

structures.name: Pulmonary Arteries
structures.fn: Carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. They are the adult circulation exception to the usual oxygen-rich artery pattern; fetal umbilical arteries also carry relatively deoxygenated blood. The pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries.
structures.clinical: Pulmonary embolism (PE): a clot, often from a DVT, lodges in the pulmonary arteries. A large saddle PE can be life-threatening.

structures.name: Carotid Arteries
structures.fn: Common carotid bifurcates at C4 into internal (brain) and external (face/scalp). Internal carotid supplies anterior 2/3 of brain.
structures.clinical: Carotid stenosis causes stroke/TIA. Carotid endarterectomy for >70% stenosis. Carotid body senses O₂/CO₂/pH.
structures.clinicalKid: Your carotid arteries are two big tubes in your neck that carry fresh blood up to your brain and your face. You can feel them gently beating on the sides of your neck, and a doctor can check that beat too. Moving your body, drinking water, and eating fruits and vegetables help keep your blood flowing strong.

structures.name: Jugular Veins
structures.fn: Internal jugular drains brain and face (runs with carotid in carotid sheath). External jugular visible on neck surface.
structures.clinical: JVD (jugular venous distension) → sign of right heart failure, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax.

structures.name: Coronary Arteries
structures.fn: LAD (left anterior descending) supplies anterior LV wall and septum ("widow maker"). LCx supplies lateral LV. RCA supplies RV and inferior LV.
structures.clinical: LAD occlusion: anterior STEMI (most dangerous). RCA occlusion: inferior MI with possible heart block.

structures.name: Femoral Artery
structures.fn: Main blood supply to lower limb. Palpable at mid-inguinal point (midway ASIS to pubic symphysis). Becomes popliteal artery behind knee.
structures.clinical: Femoral artery catheterization for angiography. Femoral artery laceration → rapid exsanguination.

structures.name: Brachial Artery
structures.fn: Continuation of axillary artery. Runs medially in arm. Blood pressure measured here (antecubital fossa). Bifurcates into radial and ulnar arteries.
structures.clinical: BP cuff occludes brachial artery (Korotkoff sounds). Supracondylar fracture may damage brachial artery → Volkmann contracture.

structures.name: Hepatic Portal Vein
structures.fn: Carries nutrient-rich blood from the GI tract and spleen to the liver for processing. Usually formed by the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
structures.clinical: Portal hypertension can cause esophageal or gastric varices, abdominal-wall collaterals, rectal varices, ascites, and splenomegaly. Rectal varices are distinct from hemorrhoids.

structures.name: Circle of Willis
structures.fn: Arterial anastomotic ring at base of brain. Formed by: anterior communicating artery connecting ACA–ACA, posterior communicating arteries connecting ICA–PCA, plus segments of ACA, ICA, and PCA. Provides collateral blood flow if one vessel is occluded. Complete circle in only ~25% of people.
structures.clinical: Berry (saccular) aneurysms: most common at anterior communicating artery junction. Rupture → subarachnoid hemorrhage ("thunderclap headache"). Congenital variants may limit collateral flow → increased stroke risk.

structures.name: Great Saphenous Vein
structures.fn: Longest vein in body. Runs from dorsum of foot, anterior to medial malleolus, up medial leg and thigh, drains into femoral vein at saphenous opening (saphenofemoral junction). Superficial position makes it accessible for cannulation and grafting.
structures.clinical: Varicose veins from incompetent valves (superficial venous insufficiency). Used as conduit for CABG (coronary artery bypass graft surgery). Saphenous nerve runs alongside — may be injured during vein stripping. DVT risk in varicosities.

structures.name: Lymphatic Vessels
structures.fn: One-way drainage system parallel to venous system. Begins as blind-ended lymph capillaries in tissues, drains through lymph nodes, collecting vessels, trunks, and ducts. Right lymphatic duct drains right upper body; thoracic duct drains everything else. Lymph propelled by skeletal muscle contraction and one-way valves.
structures.clinical: Lymphedema: impaired drainage → chronic swelling (post-surgical, filariasis in tropics). Lymphangitis: red streaking from infected lymph vessel. Sentinel lymph node biopsy for cancer staging. Chylothorax from thoracic duct injury.

nervous.name: Nervous
nervous.desc: CNS (brain + spinal cord) and PNS (31 spinal nerve pairs, 12 cranial nerve pairs, autonomic NS).

structures.name: Brain
structures.fn: ~86 billion neurons. Cerebrum (cognition, sensation, motor), cerebellum (coordination), brainstem (vital functions). Weighs ~1.4 kg, uses 20% of O₂. Protected by meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia mater) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Four lobes per hemisphere: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital.
structures.clinical: Stroke (ischemic/hemorrhagic), TBI, neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer, Parkinson), brain tumors, epilepsy. EEG measures brain waves for diagnosis of seizures, sleep disorders, and brain death.
structures.clinicalKid: Your brain is the control center for your whole body, helping you think, move, learn, and feel. Sleep, healthy food, and learning new things help it grow strong, and wearing a helmet keeps it safe.

brainWaves.characteristics: Dominant in deep NREM sleep (stage N3). Associated with growth hormone release, tissue repair, and immune system strengthening. Excessive delta in waking = brain injury or encephalopathy.
brainWaves.clinical: Abnormal waking delta waves indicate brain lesions, metabolic encephalopathy, or diffuse cortical damage. Used to assess depth of anesthesia and coma.

brainWaves.characteristics: Prominent in light sleep (N1), deep meditation, and creative insight. Hippocampal theta rhythms are critical for memory encoding and spatial navigation.
brainWaves.clinical: Excessive theta in waking = ADHD, cognitive impairment, or drowsiness. Theta bursts during memory tasks reflect hippocampal-cortical dialogue for memory consolidation.

brainWaves.characteristics: First brain wave discovered (Hans Berger, 1929). Dominant when relaxed with eyes closed. Blocked by eye opening or mental effort ("alpha blocking"). Generated primarily in the occipital cortex.
brainWaves.clinical: Reduced alpha = anxiety, insomnia. Asymmetric alpha = cortical lesion or stroke. Neurofeedback alpha training is studied for anxiety and ADHD, but blinded-trial evidence is mixed and contested, and "peak performance" uses are largely unproven.

brainWaves.characteristics: Dominant during active cognition, problem-solving, conversation, and decision-making. Sub-bands: low beta (13–15 Hz, relaxed focus), mid beta (15–20 Hz, active thinking), high beta (20–30 Hz, anxiety/excitement).
brainWaves.clinical: Excessive high beta = anxiety, stress, insomnia. Medications like benzodiazepines increase beta. Beta activity used in BCI (brain-computer interfaces) for motor imagery.

brainWaves.characteristics: Associated with sensory binding (combining sight, sound, touch into unified percepts), peak concentration, expanded consciousness, and compassion meditation. Highest frequency, lowest amplitude. Generated by fast-spiking interneurons.
brainWaves.clinical: Reduced gamma = schizophrenia, Alzheimer disease. Gamma entrainment via 40 Hz light/sound stimulation is being researched for Alzheimer treatment. Experienced meditators show elevated gamma.

sleepStages.desc: Lightest sleep — transition from wakefulness. Slow rolling eye movements, muscle tone decreasing. Hypnic jerks (myoclonic twitches) common. Easily aroused. Vertex sharp waves appear on EEG.
sleepStages.clinical: Excessive N1 = sleep fragmentation (sleep apnea, restless legs). Hypnic hallucinations may occur. Sleep onset latency measured here for narcolepsy diagnosis (MSLT test).

sleepStages.desc: True sleep begins. Core body temperature drops, heart rate slows. Sleep spindles (thalamocortical bursts) protect sleep and consolidate motor memory. K-complexes are large waveforms responding to external stimuli.
sleepStages.clinical: Sleep spindles correlate with IQ and learning ability. Reduced spindles in schizophrenia and aging. K-complexes are the brain's "sentry" — evaluating stimuli without waking.

sleepStages.desc: Deep/slow-wave sleep (SWS). Most restorative stage. Growth hormone secretion peaks. Glymphatic system clears brain waste (amyloid-β). Declarative memory consolidation occurs. Hardest to awaken from; sleep inertia if aroused.
sleepStages.clinical: Reduced N3 in aging, Alzheimer (amyloid accumulation). Sleepwalking, night terrors, and bedwetting occur during N3 arousal. Critical for immune function — sleep deprivation impairs T-cell function.

sleepStages.desc: Dreaming stage. Brain is highly active (similar to waking) but body is paralyzed (atonia via brainstem inhibition of motor neurons). Rapid conjugate eye movements. Emotional memory processing and creative problem-solving. Cycles lengthen through the night.
sleepStages.clinical: REM behavior disorder (RBD): loss of atonia → acting out dreams — strong predictor of Parkinson/Lewy body dementia. Narcolepsy: premature REM onset (SOREMPs). Nightmares occur in REM. SSRIs suppress REM sleep.

structures.name: Cerebral Cortex (4 Lobes)
structures.fn: Thin (2–4mm) outer layer of gray matter with ~16 billion neurons. 6 layers of cortical columns. Divided into 4 lobes: Frontal (executive function, motor, Broca area), Parietal (somatosensory, spatial), Temporal (auditory, Wernicke area, memory), Occipital (vision). Comprises 80% of brain mass.
structures.clinical: Frontal lobe damage: personality change (Phineas Gage case), impaired judgment. Parietal lesions: hemispatial neglect. Temporal lobe epilepsy: most common focal seizure type. Occipital stroke: cortical blindness.
structures.clinicalKid: Your cerebral cortex is the wrinkly outer layer of your brain, and it is the part that helps you think, move, see, hear, and remember. It has four areas called lobes, and each one has its own job, like seeing in the back and planning in the front. Sleep, healthy food, learning new things, and wearing a helmet keep it strong and safe.
structures.detail: Brodmann areas map 52 cytoarchitectural regions. Primary motor cortex (area 4), primary somatosensory (areas 3,1,2), primary visual (area 17), primary auditory (areas 41,42). Prefrontal cortex is last to myelinate (age ~25).

structures.name: Cerebellum
structures.fn: 10% of brain volume but contains ~80% of all neurons (~69 billion). "Little brain" at posterior fossa. Three functional divisions: vestibulocerebellum (balance), spinocerebellum (limb coordination), cerebrocerebellum (motor planning, cognition). Compares intended vs actual movement for error correction.
structures.clinical: Cerebellar lesions: ataxia (uncoordinated gait), intention tremor, dysarthria (scanning speech), nystagmus, past-pointing. Cerebellar stroke: acute vertigo and ataxia may be misdiagnosed as inner ear problems. Fetal alcohol syndrome damages cerebellum.
structures.clinicalKid: Your cerebellum is a small part at the back of your brain that helps you balance and move smoothly. It helps you walk, run, ride a bike, and catch a ball without falling over. Playing, practicing new moves, and getting good sleep help it work well.
structures.detail: Purkinje cells are among the largest neurons, each receiving ~200,000 synaptic inputs. Cerebellar cortex has 3 layers: molecular, Purkinje, granular. Emerging research shows roles in cognition, emotion, and language.

structures.name: Brainstem (Midbrain, Pons, Medulla)
structures.fn: Connects cerebrum to spinal cord. Three parts: Midbrain (visual/auditory reflexes, substantia nigra for dopamine), Pons (relay between cortex and cerebellum, respiratory rhythm), Medulla oblongata (cardiovascular center, respiratory center, vomiting, swallowing). Reticular formation spans all three — controls arousal and consciousness.
structures.clinical: Brainstem death = legal death in many jurisdictions (irreversible loss of consciousness and vital reflexes). Locked-in syndrome (ventral pons lesion): conscious but unable to move except eyes. Central sleep apnea from medullary dysfunction.
structures.clinicalKid: Your brainstem sits at the bottom of your brain, where it connects to your spinal cord. It quietly takes care of jobs you do not have to think about, like breathing, your heartbeat, and swallowing. Good sleep, healthy food, and wearing a helmet help keep it safe and working well.
structures.detail: Contains nuclei for cranial nerves III–XII. Reticular activating system (RAS) is the brain's "on switch" — damage causes coma. Decussation of pyramids in medulla: motor crossover explains contralateral motor control.

structures.name: Hippocampus
structures.fn: Seahorse-shaped structure in medial temporal lobe. Critical for converting short-term memory to long-term memory (consolidation). Contains place cells for spatial navigation (Nobel Prize 2014, O'Keefe). One of two brain regions with adult neurogenesis (new neuron formation). Theta rhythms during memory encoding.
structures.clinical: Alzheimer disease begins here — hippocampal atrophy on MRI is an early diagnostic marker. Bilateral hippocampal damage (e.g., Patient H.M.) causes severe anterograde amnesia. Chronic stress and cortisol shrink the hippocampus. PTSD associated with reduced hippocampal volume.
structures.detail: Memory replay during sleep: hippocampal neurons "replay" daytime experiences during N3 sleep, transferring memories to neocortex. Grid cells in entorhinal cortex provide spatial coordinates to hippocampal place cells.

structures.name: Amygdala
structures.fn: Almond-shaped nuclei in anterior temporal lobe. Key hub for processing fear, threat detection, and emotional memory. Receives fast "low road" input from thalamus for rapid danger response (before conscious awareness). Modulates memory storage based on emotional arousal (why emotional events are remembered better).
structures.clinical: Hyperactive amygdala in anxiety disorders, PTSD, and phobias. Bilateral amygdala damage (Urbach-Wiethe disease): inability to recognize fear in faces, impaired fear conditioning. Amygdala involved in autism spectrum disorder (social threat processing).
structures.detail: Fear conditioning pathway: auditory cortex → lateral amygdala → central amygdala → hypothalamus (stress response) + PAG (freezing). Amygdala-prefrontal interactions allow emotional regulation — basis of CBT therapy.

structures.name: Thalamus
structures.fn: Paired egg-shaped structures forming 80% of diencephalon. "Gateway to consciousness" — relays and filters ALL sensory information to cortex (except olfaction). Contains ~60 nuclei organized into functional groups. Generates sleep spindles during N2 sleep. Thalamocortical oscillations underlie consciousness itself.
structures.clinical: Thalamic stroke: contralateral sensory loss + thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy: severe, burning pain). Fatal familial insomnia: prion disease destroying thalamus → complete inability to sleep → death. Deep brain stimulation of thalamus for essential tremor.
structures.detail: Key nuclei: VPL/VPM (somatosensory relay), LGN (visual relay to V1), MGN (auditory relay to A1), pulvinar (attention), anterior nuclear group (memory, Papez circuit).

structures.name: Hypothalamus
structures.fn: Small (4g, ~1% of brain) but controls: body temperature, hunger/thirst, circadian rhythm (SCN = master clock), autonomic nervous system, pituitary gland (via hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system). Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) receives light input from retina and entrains 24-hr circadian cycle.
structures.clinical: Hypothalamic dysfunction: diabetes insipidus (no ADH), obesity (ventromedial lesion = hyperphagia), anorexia (lateral lesion = aphagia). Circadian disruption linked to depression, metabolic syndrome, cancer. Jet lag = SCN resynchronizing.
structures.detail: Thermostat analogy: anterior hypothalamus triggers cooling (vasodilation, sweating); posterior hypothalamus triggers warming (shivering, vasoconstriction). Fever = elevated set point by prostaglandins from infection.

structures.name: Corpus Callosum
structures.fn: Largest white matter structure in brain. ~200 million axons connecting left and right hemispheres. Enables interhemispheric communication and integration. Develops throughout childhood; fully myelinated by age ~12. Four regions: rostrum, genu, body, splenium.
structures.clinical: Split-brain patients (callosotomy for epilepsy): each hemisphere operates independently — left hand "doesn't know" what right hand is doing (Roger Sperry, Nobel 1981). Agenesis of corpus callosum: congenital absence, often incidental finding. Callosal lesions in MS.
structures.detail: Split-brain experiments revealed hemispheric specialization: left hemisphere = language, logic; right hemisphere = spatial, holistic processing. Information presented to one visual field is processed by contralateral hemisphere.

structures.name: Basal Ganglia
structures.fn: Deep gray matter nuclei: caudate, putamen (together = striatum), globus pallidus. With substantia nigra and subthalamic nucleus, form circuits for motor initiation/inhibition, habit formation, reward learning, and procedural memory. Direct pathway facilitates movement; indirect pathway inhibits movement.
structures.clinical: Parkinson disease: dopamine depletion in substantia nigra → bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, postural instability. Huntington disease: caudate/putamen degeneration → chorea (involuntary dance-like movements). OCD linked to caudate hyperactivity. Deep brain stimulation of subthalamic nucleus for Parkinson.
structures.detail: Dopamine from substantia nigra modulates the direct (D1, excitatory) and indirect (D2, inhibitory) pathways. Loss of this modulation in Parkinson creates the characteristic difficulty initiating movement.

structures.name: Spinal Cord
structures.fn: Extends from foramen magnum to L1–L2 (conus medullaris). Conducts sensory/motor signals. 31 segments, each with dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots.
structures.clinical: Spinal cord injury: above C4 → quadriplegia + ventilator. Complete transection → loss of motor/sensory below level.
structures.clinicalKid: Your spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerves that runs down your back inside your spine. It carries messages between your brain and the rest of your body so you can feel and move. Wearing a helmet and a seatbelt and sitting up tall help keep it safe and strong.

structures.name: Vagus Nerve (CN X)
structures.fn: Longest cranial nerve. Parasympathetic innervation to thoracic and abdominal viscera. Slows heart rate, increases GI motility, controls laryngeal muscles.
structures.clinical: Vagal stimulation: carotid sinus massage, Valsalva maneuver for SVT. Vagus nerve stimulator for epilepsy/depression. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury → hoarseness.

structures.name: Sciatic Nerve
structures.fn: Largest/longest nerve in body. L4–S3 roots. Exits pelvis through greater sciatic foramen below piriformis. Divides into tibial and common peroneal nerves above knee.
structures.clinical: Sciatica: radiculopathy from herniated disc (L4–S1). Piriformis syndrome mimics sciatica. IM injection site avoidance.
structures.clinicalKid: Your sciatic nerve is the longest, biggest nerve in your whole body, running from your lower back all the way down each leg. It carries messages between your brain and your legs so you can feel things and move, walk, and run. Stretching, moving around, and sitting up tall help your back and legs feel good.

structures.name: Brachial Plexus
structures.fn: C5–T1 nerve roots form trunks, divisions, cords, branches. Innervates entire upper limb. "Robert Taylor Drinks Cold Beer" (roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches).
structures.clinical: Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5–C6): "waiter's tip" position. Klumpke palsy (C8–T1): claw hand. Birth injuries, motorcycle accidents.

structures.name: Median Nerve
structures.fn: C5–T1 via lateral and medial cords. Motor: forearm pronators, wrist/finger flexors, thenar muscles. Sensory: palmar lateral 3.5 digits.
structures.clinical: Carpal tunnel syndrome: median nerve compression under flexor retinaculum. Hand of benediction (can't flex index/middle fingers).

structures.name: Ulnar Nerve
structures.fn: C8–T1 via medial cord. Motor: intrinsic hand muscles (interossei, hypothenar), FCU, medial FDP. Sensory: medial 1.5 digits.
structures.clinical: "Funny bone" — vulnerable at medial epicondyle. Cubital tunnel syndrome. Claw hand deformity. Froment sign.

structures.name: Femoral Nerve
structures.fn: L2–L4 via lumbar plexus. Motor: quadriceps (knee extension), iliacus, sartorius. Sensory: anterior thigh, medial leg (saphenous branch).
structures.clinical: Femoral neuropathy: difficulty climbing stairs, absent knee jerk. L4 radiculopathy mimics. Femoral nerve block for hip surgery.

structures.name: Sympathetic Chain
structures.fn: Paired paravertebral ganglia from C1 to coccyx. "Fight or flight": increases HR, dilates pupils, bronchodilation, vasoconstriction, inhibits GI.
structures.clinical: Horner syndrome (sympathetic disruption): miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis. Sympathectomy for hyperhidrosis.

structures.name: Cranial Nerves (I-XII)
structures.fn: 12 pairs: olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, spinal accessory, hypoglossal.
structures.clinical: CN III palsy: "down and out" eye, ptosis, dilated pupil. CN VII (Bell palsy): facial droop. CN XII: tongue deviates toward lesion.

lymphatic.name: Lymphatic
lymphatic.desc: Returns interstitial fluid, absorbs dietary fat, immune surveillance — 600–700 lymph nodes, thymus, spleen.

structures.name: Thymus
structures.fn: Primary lymphoid organ in anterior mediastinum. T-cell maturation and positive/negative selection. Largest in childhood, involutes after puberty (replaced by fat).
structures.clinical: Thymoma: associated with myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR antibodies). DiGeorge syndrome: thymic aplasia → T-cell deficiency.
structures.clinicalKid: Your thymus is a small organ in the middle of your chest that helps train the germ fighting cells in your body so they know how to keep you well. It does its biggest job while you are a kid, so sleep, healthy food, and exercise help your whole defense team stay strong.

structures.name: Spleen
structures.fn: Largest lymphoid organ. Filters blood: removes old RBCs (red pulp), mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens (white pulp). Stores 1/3 of platelets.
structures.clinical: Splenomegaly in mono, malaria, leukemia. Splenic rupture from trauma → emergency splenectomy. Post-splenectomy: encapsulated bacteria risk.
structures.clinicalKid: Your spleen is a soft organ on the left side of your belly that cleans your blood and takes out old, worn out blood cells. It also helps your body fight germs and keeps blood ready for when you need it. Healthy food, exercise, and washing your hands help your spleen do its job.

structures.name: Tonsils (Waldeyer Ring)
structures.fn: Pharyngeal (adenoids), palatine, tubal, and lingual tonsils form a lymphoid ring at the oropharyngeal entrance. First line of defense against inhaled/ingested pathogens.
structures.clinical: Tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess ("quinsy"). Adenoid hypertrophy → mouth breathing, sleep apnea in children.

structures.name: Cervical Lymph Nodes
structures.fn: Drain head and neck including scalp, face, oral cavity, pharynx. Deep cervical chain runs along IJV. Virchow node (left supraclavicular) drains thoracic duct.
structures.clinical: Enlarged: infection, lymphoma, metastatic cancer. Virchow node enlargement → suspect GI malignancy (Troisier sign).

structures.name: Axillary Lymph Nodes
structures.fn: 5 groups draining upper limb, breast, chest wall. Sentinel lymph node biopsy in breast cancer staging.
structures.clinical: Breast cancer staging depends on axillary LN involvement. Axillary dissection may cause lymphedema of arm.

structures.name: Inguinal Lymph Nodes
structures.fn: Superficial group drains lower limb, perineum, lower abdominal wall, external genitalia. Deep group drains along femoral vein.
structures.clinical: Lymphadenopathy in STIs, lower limb infections, lymphoma. Buboes in lymphogranuloma venereum, plague.

structures.name: Thoracic Duct
structures.fn: Main lymphatic channel (40 cm). Drains ¾ of body (everything except right upper quadrant). Empties into left subclavian/internal jugular junction (left venous angle).
structures.clinical: Chylothorax from thoracic duct injury (trauma, surgery). Milky pleural effusion with high triglycerides.

structures.name: Bone Marrow
structures.fn: Primary lymphoid organ. Red marrow produces all blood cells (hematopoiesis) including lymphocyte precursors. Adults: mainly in axial skeleton, proximal femur/humerus.
structures.clinical: Leukemia (malignant WBC proliferation). Aplastic anemia. Bone marrow biopsy from posterior iliac crest. Bone marrow transplant.

organs.name: Organ Systems
organs.desc: Major visceral organs — respiration, digestion, filtration, endocrine regulation.

structures.name: Lungs
structures.fn: Right lung: 3 lobes (superior, middle, inferior). Left lung: 2 lobes + lingula (cardiac notch). ~300 million alveoli provide ~70 m² surface area for gas exchange.
structures.clinical: Pneumonia, COPD, asthma, lung cancer (#1 cancer killer). Pneumothorax. Right bronchus more vertical → foreign body aspiration.
structures.clinicalKid: Your lungs fill up with air like two balloons when you breathe in, then push the air back out. Fresh air and exercise keep them healthy, and staying away from smoke keeps them clean.

structures.name: Liver
structures.fn: Largest internal organ (1.5 kg). 2 anatomical lobes (right larger). Functions: bile production, detoxification, protein synthesis (albumin, clotting factors), glycogen storage, drug metabolism.
structures.clinical: Hepatitis (viral A/B/C), cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma. Liver failure: jaundice, coagulopathy, encephalopathy. Transplantation.
structures.clinicalKid: Your liver is the biggest organ inside your body, and it works like a cleaning crew that filters your blood and keeps it fresh. It also helps you break down food and stores energy for later. Drinking water and eating fruits and vegetables help your liver do its job.

structures.name: Stomach
structures.fn: J-shaped muscular sac. Regions: cardia, fundus, body, antrum, pylorus. Produces HCl (pH 1–2), pepsin, intrinsic factor (B12 absorption). Capacity ~1L.
structures.clinical: Peptic ulcer disease (H. pylori, NSAIDs). Gastric cancer. GERD. Gastrectomy may cause dumping syndrome, B12 deficiency.
structures.clinicalKid: Your stomach is a stretchy bag that mixes up the food you eat and starts breaking it down. Eating slowly, chewing well, and drinking water help it do its job.

structures.name: Kidneys
structures.fn: Bean-shaped, retroperitoneal at T12–L3. Each has ~1 million nephrons. Filter 180L/day, produce 1–2L urine. Regulate fluid balance, electrolytes, acid-base, blood pressure (RAAS).
structures.clinical: CKD, nephrotic/nephritic syndrome, kidney stones, renal cell carcinoma. Right kidney lower due to liver. Dialysis when GFR <15.
structures.clinicalKid: Your kidneys are two bean shaped helpers that clean your blood and turn the waste into pee so your body can get rid of it. Drinking water and eating fruits and vegetables help them do their job. A doctor can check them to make sure they are working well.

structures.name: Small Intestine
structures.fn: 6m long: duodenum (25cm, C-shaped), jejunum (2.5m), ileum (3.5m). Primary site of nutrient absorption. Villi and microvilli increase surface area to ~200 m².
structures.clinical: Celiac disease (gluten sensitivity), Crohn disease (often terminal ileum), SBO (adhesions #1 cause), duodenal ulcers.

structures.name: Large Intestine
structures.fn: 1.5m: cecum, ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid colon, rectum. Absorbs water and electrolytes. Houses gut microbiome (~100 trillion bacteria). Forms and stores feces.
structures.clinical: Colorectal cancer (3rd most common cancer). Diverticulosis/diverticulitis. Ulcerative colitis. Appendicitis (McBurney point).

structures.name: Pancreas
structures.fn: Retroperitoneal organ. Exocrine (98%): digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, trypsinogen) and bicarbonate. Endocrine (2%): islets of Langerhans — insulin (β), glucagon (α).
structures.clinical: Acute pancreatitis (gallstones, alcohol). Pancreatic cancer (poor prognosis, 5-yr survival <10%). Type 1 diabetes (autoimmune β-cell destruction).

structures.name: Gallbladder
structures.fn: Pear-shaped sac on inferior liver surface. Stores and concentrates bile (5–10×). Contracts in response to CCK after fatty meals to release bile into duodenum.
structures.clinical: Cholelithiasis (gallstones, 10–15% of adults). Cholecystitis. Murphy sign. Cholecystectomy is one of most common surgeries.

structures.name: Urinary Bladder
structures.fn: Distensible muscular sac. Stores 400–600mL urine. Detrusor muscle contracts for micturition. Internal sphincter (involuntary), external sphincter (voluntary, pudendal nerve).
structures.clinical: UTIs (more common in females due to short urethra). Bladder cancer (painless hematuria). Neurogenic bladder in spinal cord injury.

structures.name: Diaphragm
structures.fn: Primary muscle of respiration. Dome-shaped, separates thorax from abdomen. Contracts and flattens during inspiration → negative intrathoracic pressure. Three openings: T8 (IVC), T10 (esophagus), T12 (aorta).
structures.clinical: Hiatal hernia (stomach through esophageal hiatus). Diaphragmatic paralysis from phrenic nerve injury (C3–C5). "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive."
structures.clinicalKid: Your diaphragm is a big dome-shaped muscle under your lungs that helps you breathe. When it tightens and flattens, it pulls air into your lungs, and when it relaxes, the air goes back out. Taking slow deep breaths and getting plenty of exercise help this strong muscle do its job.

structures.name: Thyroid Gland
structures.fn: Butterfly-shaped, anterior neck at C5–T1. Produces T3/T4 (metabolism, growth, development) and calcitonin (lowers blood calcium). Requires iodine.
structures.clinical: Hypothyroidism (Hashimoto): fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance. Hyperthyroidism (Graves): weight loss, tremor, exophthalmos. Thyroid nodules/cancer.

structures.name: Adrenal Glands
structures.fn: Suprarenal glands. Cortex (3 zones): zona glomerulosa (aldosterone), zona fasciculata (cortisol), zona reticularis (androgens). Medulla: epinephrine/norepinephrine.
structures.clinical: Addison disease (cortical insufficiency): hypotension, hyperpigmentation. Cushing syndrome (cortisol excess). Pheochromocytoma (medullary tumor → episodic HTN).

integumentary.name: Integumentary
integumentary.desc: Skin (largest organ, ~2m²), hair, nails, glands — barrier, thermoregulation, sensation, vitamin D synthesis.

structures.name: Epidermis
structures.fn: Outermost skin layer. 5 strata (thick skin): basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum. Keratinocytes (90%), melanocytes (8%), Langerhans cells (immune), Merkel cells (touch). Avascular — nutrients diffuse from dermis. Turnover every 28–30 days.
structures.clinical: Psoriasis: hyperproliferation (turnover 3–4 days). Melanoma from melanocyte mutation. Eczema (atopic dermatitis). Burns classified by depth of epidermal/dermal involvement.
structures.clinicalKid: Your epidermis is the thin top layer of your skin that covers your whole body like a shield and keeps germs and water out. It makes brand new cells all the time and pushes the old ones off, so your skin is always fresh. Washing with soap and water and putting on sunscreen help keep it healthy and strong.

structures.name: Dermis
structures.fn: Connective tissue layer beneath epidermis. Papillary dermis (loose CT, dermal papillae for fingerprints) and reticular dermis (dense irregular CT, collagen/elastin for strength/elasticity). Contains blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles, glands.
structures.clinical: Stretch marks (striae): torn collagen fibers. Cellulitis: bacterial infection of dermis. Dermal injection site for TB test (Mantoux). Keloid scarring from excess collagen.
structures.clinicalKid: Your dermis is the strong, stretchy layer of skin just under the surface. It is packed with tiny blood vessels, nerves, and the roots that hold your hair, and it helps your skin bend and bounce back. Drinking water and eating fruits and vegetables help keep your skin healthy and strong.

structures.name: Hypodermis (Subcutaneous)
structures.fn: Deep to dermis (not technically skin). Adipose tissue for insulation, energy storage, and mechanical cushioning. Contains large blood vessels and nerves. Subcutaneous injection site.
structures.clinical: Lipomas (benign fat tumors). Subcutaneous emphysema (air under skin, crepitus). Insulin and heparin injected subcutaneously. Obesity increases this layer.

structures.name: Hair Follicles
structures.fn: ~5 million follicles (100,000 on scalp). Hair shaft: medulla, cortex, cuticle. Arrector pili muscle causes goosebumps. Hair growth cycle: anagen (growth, 2–6 yrs), catagen (regression), telogen (rest/shedding). Stem cells in bulge region.
structures.clinical: Alopecia areata (autoimmune hair loss). Folliculitis (infected follicle). Male pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia, DHT-mediated). Hirsutism from excess androgens.

structures.name: Sweat Glands
structures.fn: Eccrine glands (~3 million): watery sweat for thermoregulation, open directly to skin surface, densest on palms/soles. Apocrine glands: thicker secretion into hair follicles in axillae/groin, active after puberty, bacterial breakdown causes body odor.
structures.clinical: Hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating). Anhidrosis in Horner syndrome. Heat stroke when sweating fails. Cystic fibrosis: elevated sweat chloride (diagnostic sweat test).

structures.name: Sebaceous Glands
structures.fn: Holocrine glands associated with hair follicles (except palms/soles). Produce sebum (lipid mixture) that waterproofs skin and hair, prevents drying, has bactericidal properties. Activity increases at puberty (androgens).
structures.clinical: Acne vulgaris: sebaceous gland hyperactivity + P. acnes bacteria + follicular plugging. Sebaceous cysts. Isotretinoin (Accutane) shrinks sebaceous glands for severe acne.

structures.name: Nails
structures.fn: Keratinized epidermal derivatives. Nail plate grows from nail matrix (under proximal fold) at ~3mm/month (fingernails) or ~1mm/month (toenails). Lunula: visible part of matrix. Nail bed highly vascular (pink color).
structures.clinical: Clubbing: sign of chronic hypoxia (lung/heart disease). Koilonychia (spoon nails): iron deficiency. Onychomycosis (fungal infection). Splinter hemorrhages: endocarditis. Beau lines: illness/stress.

structures.name: Melanocytes & Pigmentation
structures.fn: Neural crest-derived cells in stratum basale. Produce melanin (eumelanin=brown/black, pheomelanin=red/yellow) in melanosomes, transferred to surrounding keratinocytes via dendrites. UV radiation increases melanin production (tanning). Same number in all races; differences are in melanin amount/type.
structures.clinical: Vitiligo: autoimmune melanocyte destruction (depigmented patches). Albinism: defective melanin synthesis. Melanoma: deadliest skin cancer, arises from melanocytes, ABCDE criteria for detection.

respiratory.name: Respiratory
respiratory.desc: Oxygen delivery and CO₂ removal — ~12–20 breaths/min, ~6L air/min, 300 million alveoli.

structures.name: Nasal Cavity & Sinuses
structures.fn: Warms, humidifies, and filters inspired air. Nasal conchae (turbinates) increase surface area. Rich vascular plexus (Kiesselbach plexus) on septum. Paranasal sinuses (frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, sphenoid) lighten skull, add resonance to voice.
structures.clinical: Epistaxis (nosebleed): 90% anterior from Kiesselbach plexus. Sinusitis. Deviated septum. Nasal polyps in chronic rhinitis/asthma/CF. Anosmia from COVID-19.

structures.name: Pharynx
structures.fn: Muscular tube from skull base to C6. Three regions: nasopharynx (adenoids, Eustachian tube), oropharynx (palatine tonsils), laryngopharynx (diverges into esophagus and larynx). Shared airway and food passage.
structures.clinical: Pharyngitis (sore throat): viral most common, Group A Strep requires antibiotics (prevent rheumatic fever). Obstructive sleep apnea from pharyngeal collapse. Pharyngeal cancer (HPV-related rising).

structures.name: Larynx (Voice Box)
structures.fn: Cartilaginous framework at C3–C6. Thyroid cartilage (Adam's apple), cricoid (complete ring), arytenoids (move vocal cords). True vocal cords (folds) vibrate for phonation. Epiglottis closes during swallowing to protect airway.
structures.clinical: Laryngitis (hoarseness). Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (thyroid surgery) → vocal cord paralysis. Croup in children (barking cough). Laryngeal cancer from smoking. Emergency cricothyrotomy through cricothyroid membrane.

structures.name: Trachea
structures.fn: 10–12 cm tube from C6 to T4–T5 (carina). 16–20 C-shaped cartilage rings (open posteriorly to allow esophageal expansion). Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells — mucociliary escalator traps and clears particles.
structures.clinical: Tracheostomy for prolonged ventilation. Tracheomalacia (softened cartilage, floppy airway). Foreign body aspiration: right main bronchus more vertical. Tracheal intubation for general anesthesia.
structures.clinicalKid: Your windpipe is a stretchy tube in your throat that carries air down to your lungs every time you breathe. Stiff rings hold it open so air can flow, and tiny hairs inside sweep out dust to keep it clean. Fresh air and staying away from smoke help it stay healthy.

structures.name: Bronchial Tree
structures.fn: Trachea → R/L main bronchi → lobar bronchi (3R, 2L) → segmental → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles. Progressive loss of cartilage, increase in smooth muscle. ~23 generations of branching. Total cross-section increases enormously.
structures.clinical: Asthma: bronchospasm + inflammation of bronchi/bronchioles. Bronchitis: inflammation of bronchial mucosa. Bronchiectasis: permanent dilation from chronic infection. Bronchoscopy for diagnosis/biopsy.

structures.name: Alveoli
structures.fn: ~300 million alveoli provide ~70m² gas exchange surface. Type I pneumocytes (95% surface, gas exchange). Type II pneumocytes (surfactant production, reduces surface tension). Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) phagocytose particles. Blood-air barrier: 0.5μm thick.
structures.clinical: Pneumonia: alveolar infection/inflammation. ARDS: diffuse alveolar damage, pulmonary edema. Emphysema: alveolar wall destruction (COPD). Neonatal RDS: surfactant deficiency in premature infants.
structures.clinicalKid: Your alveoli are millions of tiny air pockets at the end of your lungs, and they look like little bunches of grapes. They let fresh oxygen move from the air you breathe into your blood so your whole body can use it. Breathing fresh air, exercising, and staying away from smoke help keep them clean and healthy.

structures.name: Pleura
structures.fn: Visceral pleura (covers lungs) and parietal pleura (lines chest wall) create pleural cavity containing ~5mL serous fluid. Surface tension keeps lungs expanded. Negative intrapleural pressure (−4 cmH₂O) prevents lung collapse.
structures.clinical: Pneumothorax: air in pleural space → lung collapse. Tension pneumothorax: life-threatening, mediastinal shift. Pleural effusion: fluid collection (transudate vs exudate). Mesothelioma: asbestos-related pleural cancer.

structures.name: Respiratory Muscles
structures.fn: Inspiration: diaphragm (70% of quiet breathing, C3–C5 phrenic nerve) + external intercostals. Forced inspiration adds: SCM, scalenes, pectoralis minor. Expiration: passive in quiet breathing (elastic recoil). Forced expiration: internal intercostals + abdominals.
structures.clinical: Phrenic nerve palsy → hemidiaphragm paralysis. C3–C5 spinal cord injury → respiratory failure. Myasthenia gravis: respiratory muscle weakness (myasthenic crisis). Flail chest impairs breathing mechanics.

endocrine.name: Endocrine
endocrine.desc: Hormone-producing glands — regulate metabolism, growth, reproduction, stress, homeostasis via chemical messengers.

structures.name: Pituitary Gland (Hypophysis)
structures.fn: Pea-sized "master gland" in sella turcica. Anterior (adenohypophysis): GH, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH, prolactin. Posterior (neurohypophysis): stores/releases oxytocin and ADH (made in hypothalamus). Regulated by hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones.
structures.clinical: Pituitary adenoma: visual field defect (bitemporal hemianopia from chiasm compression). Acromegaly (excess GH in adults). Hyperprolactinemia → galactorrhea, amenorrhea. Panhypopituitarism.
structures.clinicalKid: Your pituitary gland is tiny, about the size of a pea, but it is called the master gland because it sends out helpers called hormones that tell your body how to grow and feel. Good sleep, healthy food, and lots of moving and playing help it do its job. A doctor can measure how tall you are growing to check that it is working well.

structures.name: Pineal Gland
structures.fn: Small endocrine gland in epithalamus. Produces melatonin (from serotonin, regulated by light/dark cycle via SCN). Melatonin regulates circadian rhythm and has antioxidant properties. Calcifies with age (visible on X-ray as a midline marker).
structures.clinical: Pineal tumors may cause obstructive hydrocephalus (compresses cerebral aqueduct). Parinaud syndrome: upgaze palsy. Jet lag and shift-work disorder related to melatonin disruption. Exogenous melatonin used as sleep aid.

structures.name: Parathyroid Glands
structures.fn: 4 small glands on posterior thyroid surface. Produce PTH (parathyroid hormone): raises blood calcium by increasing bone resorption, renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, and activating vitamin D. PTH and calcitonin are antagonists.
structures.clinical: Hyperparathyroidism: "bones, stones, groans, and psychiatric moans" (osteoporosis, kidney stones, abdominal pain, depression). Hypoparathyroidism: hypocalcemia → tetany, Chvostek/Trousseau signs. Accidental removal during thyroidectomy.

structures.name: Islets of Langerhans
structures.fn: Endocrine clusters within pancreas (~1–2 million islets). β-cells (70%): insulin (lowers glucose). α-cells (20%): glucagon (raises glucose). δ-cells: somatostatin (inhibits both). PP-cells: pancreatic polypeptide. Islets are highly vascularized.
structures.clinical: Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune β-cell destruction (insulin-dependent). Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance + β-cell dysfunction. Insulinoma: insulin-secreting tumor → hypoglycemia. Islet transplantation research.

structures.name: Ovaries (Endocrine)
structures.fn: Produce estrogen (follicular cells) and progesterone (corpus luteum). Estrogen: secondary sex characteristics, bone density, endometrial proliferation. Progesterone: maintains pregnancy, endometrial secretion. Also produce inhibin and small amounts of testosterone.
structures.clinical: PCOS: hyperandrogenism, anovulation, polycystic ovaries. Premature ovarian failure. Menopause: estrogen decline → hot flashes, osteoporosis, cardiovascular risk. HRT replaces declining hormones.

structures.name: Testes (Endocrine)
structures.fn: Leydig cells (interstitial) produce testosterone under LH stimulation. Testosterone: male secondary sex characteristics, spermatogenesis (with FSH), muscle mass, bone density, libido. Also converted to DHT (5α-reductase) and estradiol (aromatase).
structures.clinical: Hypogonadism: low testosterone → infertility, decreased libido, osteoporosis. Testosterone replacement therapy. Anabolic steroid abuse: testicular atrophy, cardiovascular risk. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).

structures.name: Hypothalamic-Pituitary Axis
structures.fn: Master regulatory cascade. Hypothalamus releases hormones into hypophyseal portal system → anterior pituitary. Key axes: HPA (stress/cortisol), HPT (thyroid/T3/T4), HPG (gonadal/sex hormones). Negative feedback loops maintain homeostasis.
structures.clinical: HPA axis dysregulation in chronic stress, depression, PTSD. Central hypothyroidism (TSH deficiency). Kallmann syndrome: GnRH deficiency → hypogonadism + anosmia. Sheehan syndrome: pituitary necrosis postpartum.

structures.name: Adrenal Cortex Zones
structures.fn: Three zones ("GFR = salt, sugar, sex"): Glomerulosa → aldosterone (mineralocorticoid, Na⁺/K⁺ balance, RAAS). Fasciculata → cortisol (glucocorticoid, stress, anti-inflammatory). Reticularis → DHEA/androgens (weak androgens).
structures.clinical: Conn syndrome: aldosterone-secreting adenoma → hypertension, hypokalemia. Cushing syndrome: cortisol excess (moon face, buffalo hump, striae). Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency): ambiguous genitalia.

reproductive.name: Reproductive
reproductive.desc: Male and female reproductive organs — gamete production, fertilization, fetal development, hormonal regulation.

structures.name: Testes
structures.fn: Paired oval organs in scrotum (2–3°C below body temperature for spermatogenesis). Each contains ~250 lobules with seminiferous tubules (sperm production, 64–72 day cycle). Sertoli cells provide nutritive/structural support. ~200 million sperm produced daily.
structures.clinical: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis): infertility and cancer risk if uncorrected. Testicular torsion: surgical emergency (6hr window). Testicular cancer: most common solid tumor in men 15–35.

structures.name: Epididymis
structures.fn: Coiled tube (~6m uncoiled) on posterior testis. Three regions: head (receives sperm from efferent ductules), body, tail (stores mature sperm). Sperm undergo maturation during 12-day transit — gain motility and fertilizing capacity.
structures.clinical: Epididymitis: infection (STI in young men, UTI organisms in older men) → scrotal pain/swelling. Positive Prehn sign (pain relief with elevation) distinguishes from torsion. Epididymal cyst (spermatocele).

structures.name: Prostate Gland
structures.fn: Walnut-sized gland surrounding prostatic urethra below bladder. Produces ~30% of seminal fluid (citric acid, PSA, zinc, proteolytic enzymes). Five lobes; peripheral zone largest and most common site of cancer. Grows throughout life under DHT influence.
structures.clinical: BPH (benign prostatic hyperplasia): urinary obstruction in elderly men. Prostate cancer: most common male cancer, detected by PSA and DRE. Prostatitis. TURP (transurethral resection) for BPH.

structures.name: Uterus
structures.fn: Pear-shaped muscular organ. Regions: fundus, body, cervix. Three layers: endometrium (cyclically shed in menstruation), myometrium (smooth muscle, contractions during labor), perimetrium (serosa). Normally anteverted and anteflexed. Capacity expands 500× in pregnancy.
structures.clinical: Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas): most common pelvic tumor in women. Endometriosis: endometrial tissue outside uterus. Endometrial cancer (most common GYN malignancy). C-section incision through all layers.

structures.name: Ovaries
structures.fn: Paired, almond-sized organs lateral to uterus. Contain ~1–2 million oocytes at birth (depleted to ~400,000 by puberty, ~400 ovulated in lifetime). Follicular development: primordial → primary → secondary → Graafian follicle → ovulation → corpus luteum.
structures.clinical: Ovarian cysts (functional most common). Ovarian cancer: "silent killer" (often diagnosed late). PCOS. Ovarian torsion: surgical emergency. Ectopic pregnancy if fertilized egg implants in tube instead of uterus.

structures.name: Fallopian Tubes (Oviducts)
structures.fn: ~10cm tubes connecting ovaries to uterus. Regions: infundibulum (fimbriae catch ovulated oocyte), ampulla (usual site of fertilization), isthmus (narrow, connects to uterus). Ciliated epithelium and peristalsis transport ovum/embryo toward uterus over 3–4 days.
structures.clinical: Ectopic pregnancy (95% in fallopian tube): life-threatening rupture risk. PID (pelvic inflammatory disease, often from Chlamydia/Gonorrhea): scarring → infertility. Tubal ligation for permanent contraception. Salpingectomy.

structures.name: Mammary Glands
structures.fn: Modified apocrine sweat glands. 15–20 lobes of glandular tissue, each with lactiferous duct opening at nipple. Development: estrogen (ductal growth), progesterone (lobular growth), prolactin (milk production), oxytocin (milk ejection/let-down reflex).
structures.clinical: Breast cancer: most common cancer in women. BRCA1/2 gene mutations increase risk. Fibrocystic changes (benign, cyclical tenderness). Mastitis: infection during lactation. Mammography screening from age 40–50.

structures.name: Placenta
structures.fn: Temporary organ during pregnancy (develops from trophoblast). Maternal-fetal exchange: O₂, nutrients (maternal → fetal), CO₂, waste (fetal → maternal). Produces hCG, progesterone, estrogen, hPL. Barrier to most pathogens (not all: TORCH infections cross). Weighs ~500g at term.
structures.clinical: Placenta previa: placenta covers cervical os → painless bleeding. Placental abruption: premature separation → painful bleeding, emergency. Pre-eclampsia: abnormal placentation → HTN, proteinuria. hCG is the basis of pregnancy tests.

skeletal: Babies are born with about 270 bones, but adults only have 206 because many fuse together as you grow!
The smallest bone in your body is the stirrup (stapes) in your ear — it is only about 3mm long!
Bone is stronger than steel by weight — a cubic inch of bone can withstand forces of up to 19,000 pounds!
muscular: You use about 200 muscles just to take a single step when walking!
The heart is the hardest-working muscle — it beats about 100,000 times a day without ever resting.
The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in your body, and the stapedius in your ear is the smallest!
circulatory: Your blood vessels, if stretched end to end, would wrap around the Earth about 2.5 times — that is over 60,000 miles!
Your heart pumps about 2,000 gallons of blood every single day without you thinking about it.
Red blood cells live for only about 120 days, and your bone marrow makes about 2 million new ones every second!
nervous: Your brain has about 86 billion neurons, and each one can connect to up to 10,000 others — making over 100 trillion connections!
Nerve impulses travel at speeds up to 268 mph — that is faster than a Formula 1 race car!
The human brain generates about 20 watts of power — enough to light a small LED bulb!
lymphatic: Your body has about 600 to 700 lymph nodes — tiny filters that help trap germs and cancer cells!
The spleen can store up to a cup of blood as an emergency reserve for when you need it most.
Your lymphatic system moves about 3 liters of fluid back into your bloodstream every single day!
organs: Your liver performs over 500 different jobs, including making bile, filtering toxins, and storing vitamins!
The small intestine, unfolded, would be about 20 feet long — longer than most rooms!
Your kidneys filter your entire blood supply about 40 times every day — that is 180 liters of fluid!
integumentary: Your skin is your largest organ — it covers about 2 square meters and makes up about 16% of your total body weight!
You shed about 30,000 to 40,000 dead skin cells every hour — a whole new outer layer every 2 to 4 weeks!
Skin can stretch up to 3 times its original size, which is why it accommodates both growth and injury so well!
respiratory: You breathe about 22,000 times a day, moving around 11,000 liters of air through your lungs!
If you unfolded all 300 million alveoli in your lungs, the surface area would be about the size of a tennis court!
The lungs are the only organs that float on water because they are full of tiny air-filled sacs called alveoli!
endocrine: Your pituitary gland is only the size of a pea, but it controls nearly every other hormone-producing gland in your body!
Adrenaline can be released in under a second during a stressful event, instantly boosting your heart rate and strength!
The pancreas releases insulin within just minutes of you eating — it is constantly monitoring your blood sugar 24/7!
reproductive: A single human egg is the largest cell in the body and is just barely visible to the naked eye — about 0.1mm wide!
Sperm are among the smallest cells in the body — they are 10 times smaller than a red blood cell!
During pregnancy, a woman's heart grows larger and pumps about 50% more blood to support the growing baby!

data.title: Gas Exchange
data.desc: The circulatory system delivers deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where the respiratory system loads it with oxygen and offloads carbon dioxide across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane.
data.example: Every breath you take replenishes the oxygen that your red blood cells carry to every organ in your body.

data.title: Neuromuscular Junction
data.desc: Motor neurons from the nervous system release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, triggering muscle fiber contraction. Without neural signals, muscles cannot move.
data.example: When you decide to kick a soccer ball, your motor cortex sends signals down the spinal cord to fire the quadriceps muscles.

data.title: Lever System for Movement
data.desc: Muscles attach to bones via tendons and pull across joints, creating lever systems. The skeleton provides rigid levers; muscles provide the pulling force.
data.example: Your biceps pulls on the radius bone to flex your elbow — a classic third-class lever that trades force for range of motion.

data.title: Hormonal Regulation of Reproduction
data.desc: The hypothalamus-pituitary axis releases FSH and LH that regulate the gonads. Estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone from reproductive organs feedback to the endocrine system.
data.example: During puberty, rising levels of LH and FSH trigger the ovaries and testes to mature and begin producing sex hormones.

data.title: Immune Defense and Fluid Balance
data.desc: The lymphatic system returns interstitial fluid to the bloodstream and deploys immune cells made in lymphoid organs. Both systems maintain fluid homeostasis and fight infection.
data.example: When you get a cut, lymph nodes near the wound swell as they activate immune cells, while the circulatory system sends white blood cells to the site.

data.title: Hypothalamic-Pituitary Axis
data.desc: The hypothalamus bridges the nervous and endocrine systems — it integrates neural signals and translates them into hormonal commands that control the pituitary gland and all downstream hormone cascades.
data.example: When you are stressed, your hypothalamus signals the pituitary to release ACTH, which tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol.

data.title: Breathing Mechanics
data.desc: The diaphragm and intercostal muscles physically expand and compress the thoracic cavity to move air. Lungs have no muscle themselves and rely entirely on surrounding muscles.
data.example: During a deep breath, your diaphragm contracts downward and your external intercostals lift your ribs outward, creating negative pressure that pulls air in.

data.title: Sensory Receptors in Skin
data.desc: The skin contains millions of specialized nerve endings and encapsulated receptors that detect touch, pressure, temperature, and pain, feeding constant sensory data to the nervous system.
data.example: Meissner's corpuscles in your fingertips allow you to feel light touch with incredible precision, which is why you can read Braille.

data.title: Portal Circulation and Nutrient Processing
data.desc: Blood from the GI tract drains through the hepatic portal vein directly to the liver before entering general circulation, allowing the liver to process nutrients and detoxify substances first.
data.example: After you eat, glucose absorbed from the small intestine travels straight to the liver, which stores excess glucose as glycogen to prevent a blood sugar spike.

data.title: Bone Marrow Blood Cell Production
data.desc: Red bone marrow inside the skeleton is the birthplace of all blood cells. Red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets are all produced here through hematopoiesis.
data.example: The marrow in your sternum and pelvis produces about 2 million red blood cells per second to replace the ones that wear out after 120 days.

skeletal.title: The Skull
skeletal.narration: Your skull is like a super-strong helmet made of 22 fused bones. It protects your brain, houses your eyes and ears, and gives your face its shape.

skeletal.title: The Vertebral Column
skeletal.narration: Your spine is a stack of 33 vertebrae that protects your spinal cord. It holds you upright and lets you bend and twist. The S-curve acts like a spring to absorb shocks.

skeletal.title: The Rib Cage
skeletal.narration: Your 12 pairs of ribs form a protective cage around your heart and lungs. They flex slightly with each breath to let your lungs expand and contract.

skeletal.title: The Femur
skeletal.narration: The femur is your thigh bone and the longest, strongest bone in your body. It can bear loads of 2 to 3 times your body weight during walking.

skeletal.title: The Pelvis
skeletal.narration: The pelvis is a ring of bones that transfers your body weight from your spine down to your legs. It also protects your bladder and reproductive organs.

muscular.title: The Diaphragm
