muscular.narration: The diaphragm is your main breathing muscle — a dome-shaped sheet separating your chest from your abdomen. When it contracts and flattens, it creates room for your lungs to expand.

muscular.title: The Deltoid
muscular.narration: The deltoid wraps around your shoulder. Its three sections let you raise your arm to the side, swing it forward, and pull it back. Every throw, wave, and reach uses this muscle.

muscular.title: Rectus Abdominis
muscular.narration: The rectus abdominis creates the six-pack appearance. It flexes your trunk forward and helps stabilize your pelvis when you walk and run.

muscular.title: The Quadriceps
muscular.narration: Your quadriceps are four powerful muscles on the front of your thigh. They straighten your knee and are critical for walking, climbing stairs, and running.

muscular.title: The Gastrocnemius
muscular.narration: The gastrocnemius is the big calf muscle on the back of the lower leg. It points your foot down for push-off when walking, connecting to the heel via the Achilles tendon.

circulatory.title: The Heart
circulatory.narration: Your heart is a fist-sized pump that beats about 100,000 times every day. The right side sends blood to the lungs; the left pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body.

circulatory.title: The Aorta
circulatory.narration: The aorta is the biggest artery in your body. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle, arches over your heart, then descends to supply every organ.

circulatory.title: Coronary Arteries
circulatory.narration: The coronary arteries are the heart's own blood supply. When one gets blocked by a clot, that part of the heart is starved of oxygen — that is a heart attack.

circulatory.title: The Carotid Arteries
circulatory.narration: You have two carotid arteries, one on each side of your neck. They are the main highways carrying blood to your brain. You can feel them pulsing in your neck.

nervous.title: The Brain
nervous.narration: Your brain is command central for your entire body, with about 86 billion neurons. The outer cortex handles thinking and senses. The cerebellum coordinates balance and movement.

nervous.title: The Cerebral Cortex
nervous.narration: The cortex is the wrinkled outer layer of your brain. The front plans and controls movement. The back processes vision. The sides handle sound and memory.

nervous.title: The Spinal Cord
nervous.narration: The spinal cord is the main highway of your nervous system, running inside the vertebral column. Messages travel up and down it thousands of times every second.

nervous.title: The Vagus Nerve
nervous.narration: The vagus nerve wanders from your brain stem all the way to your abdomen. It controls heart rate, digestion, and breathing as part of your rest-and-digest response.

lymphatic.title: The Thymus
lymphatic.narration: The thymus is where immature T-cells learn to tell the difference between your own cells and foreign invaders. It is most active during childhood and shrinks after puberty.

lymphatic.title: The Spleen
lymphatic.narration: The spleen filters old and damaged red blood cells out of your blood and helps your immune system respond to blood-borne bacteria and viruses.

lymphatic.title: Cervical Lymph Nodes
lymphatic.narration: Lymph nodes along your neck filter lymph fluid and trap germs draining from your head and throat. They swell and become tender when you have a sore throat.

lymphatic.title: Bone Marrow
lymphatic.narration: Deep inside your larger bones is red bone marrow, a factory that produces all your blood cells — billions of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets every hour.

organs.title: The Lungs
organs.narration: Your two lungs fill most of your chest cavity. Inside are about 300 million tiny alveoli where oxygen enters your blood and carbon dioxide leaves.

organs.title: The Liver
organs.narration: The liver performs over 500 functions: making bile to digest fat, filtering toxins, storing sugar as glycogen, and producing essential proteins.

organs.title: The Stomach
organs.narration: Your stomach is a muscular J-shaped bag that churns food with acid and digestive enzymes, breaking it into a paste that slowly enters the small intestine.

organs.title: The Kidneys
organs.narration: Your two kidneys each contain about a million tiny filters called nephrons. Together they filter all your blood about 40 times a day, removing waste and regulating fluid balance.

integumentary.title: The Epidermis
integumentary.narration: The epidermis is the outermost layer of your skin — a waterproof barrier you can see and touch. It renews itself completely about every 28 days.

integumentary.title: The Dermis
integumentary.narration: Just below the epidermis is the dermis, packed with collagen fibers, blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands, and hair follicles. It gives skin its strength and elasticity.

integumentary.title: Hair Follicles
integumentary.narration: Each hair grows from a follicle deep in your skin. A tiny muscle attached to the follicle causes hair to stand up when you are cold or scared, creating goosebumps.

integumentary.title: Melanocytes
integumentary.narration: Melanocytes produce melanin, the pigment that gives skin and hair their color. UV light triggers them to make more melanin to protect your DNA — that is what a tan actually is.

respiratory.title: Nasal Cavity
respiratory.narration: Your nose warms, humidifies, and filters the air before it reaches your lungs. Inside, turbinate bones create turbulence that maximizes contact with mucous membranes.

respiratory.title: The Larynx
respiratory.narration: The larynx, or voice box, sits at the top of your trachea. Two vocal cords inside vibrate as air passes over them to create sound.

respiratory.title: The Bronchial Tree
respiratory.narration: The trachea splits into bronchi, which branch again and again like a tree into smaller tubes. By the time air reaches the alveoli, it has traveled through about 23 generations of branching.

respiratory.title: The Alveoli
respiratory.narration: The alveoli are 300 million tiny balloon-like sacs at the end of the bronchial tree. Oxygen crosses into the blood and carbon dioxide crosses out in less than a second.

endocrine.title: The Pituitary Gland
endocrine.narration: The pituitary is a pea-sized gland at the base of your brain. It is called the master gland because it sends hormonal commands to your thyroid, adrenals, gonads, and other glands.

endocrine.title: The Thyroid
endocrine.narration: The thyroid gland wraps around the front of your trachea in a butterfly shape. It produces hormones that control your metabolic rate — how fast your cells burn energy.

endocrine.title: Adrenal Cortex
endocrine.narration: Sitting on top of each kidney, the adrenal glands produce steroid hormones. The cortex makes cortisol for stress and aldosterone for salt balance. The medulla releases adrenaline in emergencies.

endocrine.title: Islets of Langerhans
endocrine.narration: Scattered in the pancreas, beta cells make insulin to lower blood sugar and alpha cells make glucagon to raise it. Together they keep your blood glucose in a narrow safe range.

reproductive.title: The Testes
reproductive.narration: The testes are located in the scrotum where the temperature is 2 to 3 degrees cooler than the body, essential for sperm production. Each day they produce about 200 million sperm.

reproductive.title: The Uterus
reproductive.narration: The uterus is a muscular pear-shaped organ where a fertilized egg implants and grows into a baby. Its inner lining thickens each month and sheds during menstruation if no egg implants.

reproductive.title: The Ovaries
reproductive.narration: The two ovaries contain all the eggs a female will ever have. Each month, one egg matures and is released at ovulation, ready to be fertilized in the fallopian tube.

reproductive.title: The Placenta
reproductive.narration: The placenta develops during pregnancy, connecting mother and baby without their blood mixing. It transfers oxygen and nutrients to the baby while removing carbon dioxide and waste.

data.title: The Runner's Knee
data.presentation: A 16-year-old cross-country runner has dull aching pain around the front of the knee that worsens going down stairs and after long runs. No swelling or locking. Pain improves with rest.
data.question: Which structure is most likely affected?
data.explanation: Patellofemoral pain syndrome occurs when the patella does not track smoothly in its groove on the femur. Repeated stress from running causes cartilage irritation. Treatment includes quad strengthening, hip stabilization, and activity modification.

data.title: The Shoulder That Won't Lift
data.presentation: A 45-year-old painter has gradual onset right shoulder pain for 3 months. He cannot lift his arm above 90 degrees without pain. He wakes up at night with shoulder pain and a grinding sensation.
data.question: Which structure is most likely torn?
data.explanation: The supraspinatus is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle. It runs under the acromion where it is susceptible to impingement and tears. Overhead work like painting increases this risk significantly.

data.title: Racing Heart After Exercise
data.presentation: A 14-year-old athlete notices her heart racing and skipping beats for a few seconds after sprinting. She feels fine otherwise, with no chest pain or fainting. Physical exam is normal.
data.question: Which structure controls the normal heart rhythm?
data.explanation: The SA node in the right atrium is the heart's natural pacemaker. During intense exercise, adrenaline can cause benign palpitations as the heart rate adjusts. Persistent arrhythmias should be evaluated to rule out structural heart disease.

data.title: The Numb Hand
data.presentation: A 35-year-old office worker has progressive tingling and numbness in her thumb, index, and middle fingers for 2 months, worse at night. She shakes her hand to relieve it. She types 8 hours a day.
data.question: Which nerve is being compressed?
data.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum at the wrist. The median nerve supplies sensation to the thumb and first 3.5 fingers. Repetitive wrist use is a major risk factor.

data.title: The Swollen Neck Node
data.presentation: A 17-year-old presents with a 3 cm painless, rubbery lymph node in the left neck for 6 weeks. He has had night sweats and lost 5 kg without trying. No fever or sore throat.
data.question: What diagnosis must be urgently ruled out?
data.explanation: Painless lymphadenopathy with B-symptoms (night sweats, weight loss, fever) is the classic presentation of Hodgkin lymphoma in young adults. Biopsy showing Reed-Sternberg cells confirms the diagnosis.

data.title: The Diabetic Emergency
data.presentation: A 16-year-old with known Type 1 diabetes is found confused at home, breathing deeply and rapidly. His breath smells fruity. Blood glucose is 480 mg/dL. He missed his insulin doses for 2 days.
data.question: Which cells failed, and what is the emergency condition?
data.answer: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets; diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
data.explanation: With too little insulin, many tissues cannot use glucose normally and the liver increases ketone production from fat. Ketones accumulate and acidify the blood; deep Kussmaul breathing helps lower carbon dioxide. DKA is a medical emergency treated with fluids, insulin, electrolyte monitoring, and correction of the trigger.

data.title: The Broken Collarbone
data.presentation: An 11-year-old falls off his bicycle and lands on his outstretched right hand. He has immediate pain and deformity at the middle third of his right clavicle. He holds his arm close to his side.
data.question: Why is the middle third of the clavicle the most common fracture site?
data.answer: The middle third is thinnest and has no muscular reinforcement
data.explanation: The clavicle is the most frequently fractured bone. Its middle third is thinnest and lacks muscular protection. Force from a fall on an outstretched hand concentrates at this weak point. Most heal with sling immobilization.

data.title: Breathless at High Altitude
data.presentation: A healthy 15-year-old hikes to 12,000 feet and develops headache, shortness of breath at rest, and a dry cough. Her oxygen saturation is 84%. At sea level it was 99%.
data.question: Why does altitude cause these symptoms, and which structure is most stressed?
data.answer: The alveoli and respiratory muscles; reduced atmospheric oxygen causes hypoxia
data.explanation: At high altitude, atmospheric pressure drops, reducing the partial pressure of oxygen. Less oxygen crosses the alveolar membrane. The body compensates by breathing faster and deeper, increasing respiratory muscle work.

data.title: Path of Blood
data.desc: Follow a red blood cell through the entire circulatory system.

steps.label: Right Atrium
steps.detail: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the superior and inferior vena cava.

steps.label: Right Ventricle
steps.detail: Blood passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it toward the lungs.

steps.label: Pulmonary Arteries
steps.detail: The right ventricle ejects blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries toward both lungs.

steps.label: Lung Capillaries
steps.detail: In the alveolar capillaries, CO2 is released and O2 is picked up through the thin alveolar membrane.

steps.label: Pulmonary Veins
steps.detail: Freshly oxygenated blood returns to the heart via the four pulmonary veins.

steps.label: Left Atrium
steps.detail: The four pulmonary veins empty oxygenated blood into the left atrium, which fills and then pushes it through the mitral valve.

steps.label: Left Ventricle
steps.detail: Blood passes through the mitral valve into the muscular left ventricle, the strongest heart chamber.

steps.label: Aorta
steps.detail: The left ventricle powerfully ejects blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, the body's main highway.

steps.label: Body Tissues
steps.detail: Arteries branch into arterioles and capillaries where O2 and nutrients are delivered and CO2/waste collected.

steps.label: Venous Return
steps.detail: Deoxygenated blood returns through venules and veins, assisted by muscle pumps and valves, back to the right atrium.

data.title: Path of Air
data.desc: Trace the journey of a breath of air from nose to alveoli and back.

steps.label: Nasal Cavity
steps.detail: Air enters through the nostrils and is warmed, humidified, and filtered by mucous membranes and turbinates.

steps.label: Pharynx
steps.detail: Air passes through the nasopharynx and oropharynx, a shared passage with the digestive tract.

steps.label: Larynx
steps.detail: Air crosses the vocal cords in the voice box. The epiglottis guards against food entering the airway.

steps.label: Trachea
steps.detail: The trachea (windpipe) is reinforced by C-shaped cartilage rings. Cilia move mucus upward to trap debris.

steps.label: Bronchi
steps.detail: The trachea splits into left and right main bronchi, each entering a lung. They branch into smaller bronchioles.

steps.label: Alveoli
steps.detail: 300 million grape-like sacs where gas exchange occurs. O2 diffuses into blood; CO2 diffuses out. Surface area equals a tennis court.

steps.label: Exhalation
steps.detail: The diaphragm relaxes and rises, reducing lung volume. CO2-rich air is pushed out through the same pathway in reverse.

data.title: Path of Food
data.desc: Follow a meal from mouth through the entire digestive system.

steps.label: Mouth
steps.detail: Teeth mechanically break food down. Salivary amylase begins starch digestion. The tongue shapes food into a bolus.

steps.label: Pharynx & Esophagus
steps.detail: Swallowing pushes the bolus past the epiglottis. Peristaltic waves move it down the 25cm esophagus in about 8 seconds.

steps.label: Stomach
steps.detail: Gastric acid (pH 1.5-3.5) and pepsin break down proteins. Churning produces chyme over 2-4 hours.

steps.label: Duodenum
steps.detail: The first 25cm of the small intestine receives bile from the liver/gallbladder and enzymes from the pancreas.

steps.label: Jejunum & Ileum
steps.detail: Most nutrient absorption occurs here via villi and microvilli, increasing surface area 600-fold. 6-7 meters long.

steps.label: Large Intestine
steps.detail: Water and electrolytes are reabsorbed. Gut bacteria ferment remaining fiber, producing vitamins K and B12.

steps.label: Rectum & Excretion
steps.detail: Waste is compacted and stored in the rectum until defecation. The entire journey takes 24-72 hours.

data.title: Path of a Nerve Signal
data.desc: Trace a reflex arc from stimulus to response.

steps.label: Receptor
steps.detail: A sensory receptor in the skin detects a painful stimulus (like touching a hot surface) and generates an electrical signal.

steps.label: Sensory Neuron
steps.detail: The signal travels along a sensory (afferent) neuron toward the spinal cord at up to 120 m/s via saltatory conduction.

steps.label: Spinal Cord
steps.detail: In the dorsal horn, the sensory neuron synapses with an interneuron. For reflexes, the signal does not need to reach the brain.

steps.label: Interneuron
steps.detail: The interneuron in the spinal gray matter integrates the signal and relays it to a motor neuron.

steps.label: Motor Neuron
steps.detail: The motor (efferent) neuron carries the command signal from the ventral horn down to the target muscle.

steps.label: Effector (Muscle)
steps.detail: Acetylcholine released at the neuromuscular junction causes muscle contraction. You pull your hand away before feeling pain.

steps.label: Brain Awareness
steps.detail: Meanwhile, a copy of the signal ascends to the somatosensory cortex. You consciously feel pain about 0.5 seconds after the reflex.

exercise.title: Exercise: force to gas exchange
exercise.subtitle: Trace how four body systems coordinate when you climb a flight of stairs.

perturbation.title: Pulmonary edema
perturbation.change: Fluid increases the distance between alveolar air and capillary blood.
perturbation.localEffect: Oxygen diffusion falls despite continued ventilation.
perturbation.systemEffect: Working muscle receives less oxygen, so fatigue and breathlessness can increase.

intervention.title: Respond to the oxygen-delivery bottleneck
intervention.prompt: Which response best addresses the disrupted link without increasing oxygen demand?

options.label: Reduce demand and support gas exchange
options.local: Lower demand and improved alveolar-capillary transfer reduce the supply-demand mismatch.
options.system: More usable oxygen can reach working muscle while the fluid-related barrier problem is addressed.
options.why: This response targets the limiting respiratory handoff and avoids adding more muscular demand.

options.label: Increase exercise intensity
options.local: Muscle oxygen demand rises while diffusion remains limited.
options.system: The delivery gap widens, making fatigue and breathlessness more likely.
options.why: This increases demand upstream of an unresolved gas-exchange bottleneck.

options.label: Focus only on muscle force
options.local: Cross-bridge cycling continues, but oxygen loading remains impaired.
options.system: The respiratory bottleneck still limits the whole exercise pathway.
options.why: Improving force generation alone does not repair the disrupted alveolar-capillary transfer step.

synthesis.headline: Exercise is a coordinated demand-and-supply loop: force raises demand, circulation delivers, and the lungs refresh the blood.
synthesis.typical: Typical response: motor units generate force while cardiac output, local blood flow, ventilation, and perfusion rise together.
synthesis.disrupted: Pulmonary edema: a thicker air-blood barrier interrupts oxygen delivery even when the muscles, heart, and ventilatory drive are active.
synthesis.takeaway: The limiting step in one system can become the bottleneck for the entire exercise response.

steps.title: Generate force
steps.trigger: Acetylcholine starts a muscle-fiber action potential.
steps.mechanism: Calcium exposes actin sites so myosin cross-bridges cycle.
steps.outcome: Sarcomeres shorten and tendon tension rises.
steps.advanced: Calcium binds troponin, shifts tropomyosin, and permits ATP-dependent cross-bridge cycling; force depends on motor-unit recruitment and firing frequency.
steps.summary: Motor signals produce sarcomere shortening and skeletal-muscle tension.
steps.question: What directly produces active tension inside a muscle fiber?
steps.feedback: Cross-bridge cycling pulls actin past myosin, shortening sarcomeres and generating tension.

steps.title: Move the joint
steps.trigger: Tendon tension reaches the bones around the knee.
steps.mechanism: Force acting at a moment arm creates joint torque.
steps.outcome: The knee changes angle while cartilage spreads compressive load.
steps.advanced: Net joint torque reflects muscle force, moment-arm length, gravity, and opposing muscle activity; the patella improves the quadriceps moment arm.
steps.summary: Tendon force crosses the knee and rotates bones around the joint while cartilage distributes load.
steps.question: How does muscle tension become visible joint movement?
options: Tendon pull creates torque around the joint
Ligaments actively shorten to pull the bones
Pressurized synovial fluid pushes the tibia forward
steps.feedback: A contracting muscle transmits force through its tendon, creating torque around the joint axis.

steps.title: Increase delivery
steps.trigger: Working muscle raises oxygen demand and metabolite production.
steps.mechanism: Heart rate and stroke volume rise while active-muscle arterioles dilate.
steps.outcome: Cardiac output and local blood flow increase.
steps.advanced: Cardiac output equals heart rate × stroke volume; sympathetic drive raises both while local metabolites help redistribute flow toward active tissue.
steps.summary: Cardiac output rises so working tissue receives more oxygenated blood and removes more carbon dioxide.
steps.question: Which cardiovascular change best supports exercising muscle?
options: Lower blood flow to active tissue
steps.feedback: Higher heart rate and stroke volume increase cardiac output and support blood flow to active muscle.

steps.title: Exchange gases
steps.trigger: Exercise increases oxygen extraction and carbon-dioxide delivery to the lungs.
steps.mechanism: Ventilation and perfusion maintain steep partial-pressure gradients.
steps.outcome: Oxygen enters blood while carbon dioxide leaves it.
steps.advanced: Diffusion follows partial-pressure gradients and depends on surface area, membrane thickness, and gas properties; matched ventilation and perfusion improve exchange.
steps.summary: Ventilation and pulmonary blood flow sustain diffusion across the thin alveolar-capillary barrier.
steps.question: What keeps oxygen moving from alveolar air into blood?
options: Equal oxygen pressure maintained on both sides
steps.feedback: Ventilation and perfusion maintain an oxygen partial-pressure gradient across a very thin barrier.

meal.title: After a meal: absorption to delivery
meal.subtitle: Follow water-soluble nutrients from the intestinal surface through portal blood, liver processing, and systemic circulation.

perturbation.title: Villous atrophy
perturbation.change: Shortened villi and damaged brush border reduce absorptive surface area.
perturbation.localEffect: Fewer nutrients, electrolytes, and water cross efficiently.
perturbation.systemEffect: Portal nutrient delivery falls and malabsorption can affect tissues throughout the body.

intervention.title: Respond to the absorption bottleneck
intervention.prompt: Which response best supports the first disrupted handoff in this pathway?

options.label: Support mucosal recovery and absorbable intake
options.local: Preserving functional epithelium and usable substrates supports the remaining transport surface.
options.system: Portal nutrient delivery can recover as intestinal absorption improves.
options.why: This addresses the damaged absorption interface where the pathway first fails.

options.label: Increase portal flow alone
options.local: More blood passes beneath villi, but the damaged surface still limits transfer into capillaries.
options.system: The liver still receives less absorbed substrate than expected.
options.why: Downstream flow cannot replace the missing epithelial transport step.

options.label: Block remaining nutrient transporters
options.local: Even fewer solutes cross surviving enterocytes.
options.system: Portal delivery and whole-body nutrient availability fall further.
options.why: This directly weakens the remaining functional absorption route.

synthesis.headline: A meal becomes useful through a sequence of transport, first-pass processing, and controlled systemic delivery.
synthesis.typical: Typical response: villus capillaries collect water-soluble nutrients, portal blood reaches hepatocytes, and the heart distributes the processed supply.
synthesis.disrupted: Villous atrophy: reduced surface area weakens the first handoff, so later liver processing and tissue delivery receive less substrate.
synthesis.takeaway: Absorption is not the end of digestion; it is the entry point for whole-body metabolic coordination.

steps.title: Absorb nutrients
steps.trigger: Digestion produces absorbable monosaccharides and amino acids near the brush border.
steps.mechanism: Apical and basolateral transporters move solutes across enterocytes.
steps.outcome: Water-soluble nutrients enter villus capillary blood.
steps.advanced: Sodium-coupled transport drives uptake of glucose and many amino acids; basolateral carriers release them into interstitial fluid and capillaries.
steps.summary: Monosaccharides and amino acids cross enterocytes and enter capillaries inside each intestinal villus.
steps.question: Where do most absorbed sugars and amino acids enter first?
steps.feedback: Water-soluble nutrients enter villus capillaries; most long-chain dietary fats take the lacteal and lymph route.

steps.title: Reach the liver
steps.trigger: Villus capillaries drain nutrient-rich blood from the intestine.
steps.mechanism: Mesenteric veins converge into the hepatic portal circulation.
steps.outcome: Absorbed solutes reach liver sinusoids before systemic circulation.
steps.advanced: Portal flow provides first-pass exposure of hepatocytes to nutrients, hormones, and some orally absorbed substances before blood returns through hepatic veins.
steps.summary: Nutrient-rich venous blood from the intestine travels to liver lobules through the hepatic portal vein.
steps.question: Why does portal blood reach the liver before the general circulation?
options: To bypass metabolism until nutrients are needed
To allow early processing and storage
steps.feedback: The portal route gives hepatocytes early access to absorbed nutrients for storage, transformation, and controlled release.

steps.title: Process the meal
steps.trigger: Post-meal substrates and insulin reach hepatocytes through sinusoidal blood.
steps.mechanism: Hepatocytes take up glucose and other nutrients for storage or transformation.
steps.outcome: Nutrient peaks are buffered before controlled systemic release.
steps.advanced: Insulin favors hepatic glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis; hepatocytes also process amino acids, lipids, drugs, and plasma-protein precursors.
steps.summary: Hepatocytes take up nutrients across sinusoids, store some, transform others, and help stabilize blood composition.
steps.question: Which liver response helps buffer a rise in blood glucose after a meal?
steps.feedback: Hepatocytes can convert glucose to glycogen for storage and later release glucose when the body needs it.

steps.title: Deliver nutrients
steps.trigger: Processed hepatic blood returns through hepatic veins and the vena cava.
steps.mechanism: The heart sends blood through pulmonary then left-heart circulation.
steps.outcome: The aorta distributes nutrients and oxygen to body tissues.
steps.advanced: Hepatic venous blood joins systemic venous return, passes through pulmonary circulation, and is ejected by the left ventricle into the aorta.
steps.summary: Processed blood returns to the heart and enters systemic circulation, distributing nutrients to tissues.
steps.question: What is the next destination after blood leaves the left ventricle?
steps.feedback: The left ventricle ejects blood through the aorta into systemic arteries that supply body tissues.

wound.title: Wound repair: perfusion to rebuilding
wound.subtitle: Trace how circulating blood supports clot formation, immune cleanup, and restoration of the skin barrier.

perturbation.title: Impaired wound healing
perturbation.change: Poor perfusion and prolonged inflammation delay the rebuilding phase.
perturbation.localEffect: Keratinocyte migration, angiogenesis, and matrix deposition slow.
perturbation.systemEffect: The wound stays open longer and becomes more vulnerable to infection and breakdown.

intervention.title: Respond to the repair bottleneck
intervention.prompt: Which response best supports progression from inflammation into rebuilding?

options.label: Improve perfusion and support orderly repair
options.local: Repair cells receive oxygen and substrates while inflammation can resolve toward rebuilding.
options.system: Keratinocyte migration, angiogenesis, and matrix deposition are better supported.
options.why: This restores the supply and transition conditions required by the rebuilding phase.

options.label: Sustain inflammation indefinitely
options.local: Proteases and inflammatory signals continue to dominate the wound environment.
options.system: Matrix formation and epithelial closure remain delayed.
options.why: Inflammation is useful early, but failure to transition can obstruct later repair.

options.label: Suppress new vessel growth
options.local: Granulation tissue receives less oxygen and fewer circulating resources.
options.system: The open wound remains poorly supported and closes more slowly.
options.why: Angiogenesis is a core component of the proliferative repair phase.

synthesis.headline: Repair is an overlapping relay: blood supplies the materials, clotting seals the breach, immune cells clear it, and skin rebuilds.
synthesis.typical: Typical response: perfusion supports hemostasis, inflammation resolves toward repair, and new epithelium grows over a vascular matrix.
synthesis.disrupted: Impaired healing: poor perfusion or prolonged inflammation slows the rebuilding handoff and leaves the barrier vulnerable.
synthesis.takeaway: A wound is a systems problem as well as a local skin problem.

steps.title: Supply the tissue
steps.trigger: Tissue injury disrupts local vessels and raises metabolic demand.
steps.mechanism: Remaining and newly recruited microvessels deliver blood components.
steps.outcome: Repair cells receive oxygen, substrates, and circulating partners.
steps.advanced: Perfusion supports oxidative metabolism and leukocyte delivery; ischemia, edema, or vascular disease can slow every subsequent repair phase.
steps.summary: Systemic blood flow supplies oxygen, platelets, immune cells, and nutrients near the injured tissue.
steps.question: Why is adequate perfusion important before tissue rebuilding begins?
options: It delivers repair cells and oxygen
It prevents any inflammation from starting
steps.feedback: Perfusion delivers oxygen, nutrients, platelets, and circulating immune cells needed across repair phases.

steps.title: Stop blood loss
steps.trigger: Exposed collagen and tissue factor signal vessel damage.
steps.mechanism: Platelets aggregate while the coagulation cascade generates fibrin.
steps.outcome: A stabilized clot limits blood loss and forms a temporary matrix.
steps.advanced: Platelet adhesion and activation amplify recruitment, while thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin that cross-links the provisional plug.
steps.summary: Vasoconstriction, platelet activation, and fibrin formation create a temporary wound seal and scaffold.
steps.question: What stabilizes the initial platelet plug?
steps.feedback: The coagulation cascade produces fibrin strands that reinforce the platelet plug and temporary matrix.

steps.title: Clear damage
steps.trigger: Damage signals and microbial products create chemotactic gradients.
steps.mechanism: Neutrophils arrive early; macrophages continue phagocytosis and signaling.
steps.outcome: Debris is cleared and repair programs are activated.
steps.advanced: Macrophage signaling helps shift the wound from a pro-inflammatory state toward fibroblast activity, angiogenesis, and matrix deposition.
steps.summary: Neutrophils and macrophages remove microbes and debris while coordinating the transition toward repair.
steps.question: Which cell helps continue cleanup and signals later repair?
steps.feedback: Macrophages clear debris and release signals that recruit fibroblasts, support angiogenesis, and coordinate repair.

steps.title: Rebuild the barrier
steps.trigger: Growth factors signal surviving epithelial and connective-tissue cells.
steps.mechanism: Keratinocytes migrate, fibroblasts deposit matrix, and capillaries sprout.
steps.outcome: The surface closes over vascular granulation tissue.
steps.advanced: Re-epithelialization restores barrier continuity while fibroblasts generate provisional extracellular matrix; later remodeling reorganizes collagen and reduces vascularity.
steps.summary: Keratinocytes close the surface while fibroblasts deposit matrix and new vessels support granulation tissue.
steps.question: Which paired processes directly restore the wound surface and support tissue beneath it?
options: Cardiac valve closure and hepatic bile flow
steps.feedback: Migrating keratinocytes restore the epithelial barrier while angiogenesis supplies the rebuilding tissue.

fluid.title: Fluid balance: perfusion to concentration
fluid.subtitle: Follow blood from cardiac delivery through renal filtration, tubular recovery, and final urine concentration.

perturbation.title: Glomerular barrier injury
perturbation.change: The filtration barrier becomes abnormally permeable to plasma proteins.
perturbation.localEffect: Protein enters Bowman space and the tubular filtrate.
perturbation.systemEffect: Urinary protein loss can lower plasma oncotic pressure and contribute to edema.

intervention.title: Respond to the filtration bottleneck
intervention.prompt: Which response best protects the pathway when barrier selectivity is impaired?

options.label: Protect barrier selectivity and track fluid loss
options.local: Reducing further barrier stress limits additional protein escape into filtrate.
options.system: Preserving plasma proteins supports oncotic pressure and fluid distribution.
options.why: This targets the abnormal permeability that begins the downstream fluid imbalance.

options.label: Force more filtration pressure
options.local: Greater pressure can drive more fluid and protein across an injured barrier.
options.system: Protein loss and edema risk can worsen rather than improve.
options.why: More filtration is not beneficial when the filter has lost selectivity.

options.label: Block all tubular reabsorption
options.local: Useful water and solutes remain in tubular fluid instead of returning to blood.
options.system: Volume and electrolyte losses add a second homeostatic disruption.
options.why: Tubular recovery remains essential even when the glomerular barrier is injured.

synthesis.headline: Fluid balance depends on a controlled pipeline from perfusion to filtration, selective recovery, and final concentration.
synthesis.typical: Typical response: cardiac delivery supplies glomeruli, the barrier filters small solutes, tubules recover essentials, and ADH tunes water loss.
synthesis.disrupted: Glomerular barrier injury: protein leaks into filtrate, changing the composition of tubular fluid and contributing to downstream fluid imbalance.
synthesis.takeaway: Kidneys regulate the internal environment by changing both what leaves blood and what returns to it.

steps.title: Deliver renal blood
steps.trigger: Systemic arterial pressure drives blood toward the renal arteries.
steps.mechanism: Cardiac output and renal vascular tone establish renal blood flow.
steps.outcome: Blood reaches glomerular capillaries for regulated filtration.
steps.advanced: At rest, the kidneys receive roughly one-fifth of cardiac output; autoregulation helps stabilize renal blood flow across a range of arterial pressures.
steps.summary: Cardiac delivery and renal vascular resistance determine how much blood reaches the filtration apparatus.
steps.question: Which vessels carry systemic arterial blood directly toward the kidneys?
steps.feedback: Renal arteries branch from the abdominal aorta and supply progressively smaller vessels leading to afferent arterioles.

steps.title: Filter plasma
steps.trigger: Hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid against the glomerular filtration barrier.
steps.mechanism: Fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, and podocyte slits select what crosses.
steps.outcome: Water and small solutes enter Bowman space while cells and most proteins remain in blood.
steps.advanced: Net filtration reflects glomerular hydrostatic pressure opposed by capsular pressure and plasma oncotic pressure; barrier size and charge selectivity restrict proteins.
steps.summary: The glomerulus produces a cell-poor, nearly protein-free ultrafiltrate from plasma.
steps.question: Which component is normally retained most strongly by an intact filtration barrier?
steps.feedback: Blood cells and most plasma proteins are retained, while water and many small solutes enter the filtrate.

steps.title: Recover essentials
steps.trigger: Filtered fluid enters the proximal tubule with valuable solutes and water.
steps.mechanism: Selective transport returns sodium, glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, and water to capillary blood.
steps.outcome: Most filtered volume and useful solutes rejoin the circulation.
steps.advanced: The proximal tubule performs bulk reabsorption; active sodium transport creates electrochemical and osmotic gradients that support coupled solute and water recovery.
steps.summary: Tubular transport prevents essential filtered substances from being lost in urine.
steps.question: Why does water often follow sodium reabsorption?
options: Water is actively pumped by myosin
steps.feedback: Solute recovery changes osmotic gradients, so water follows passively through and between tubular cells.

steps.title: Concentrate urine
steps.trigger: Hydration state changes antidiuretic hormone signaling and collecting-duct permeability.
steps.mechanism: The medullary osmotic gradient draws water from collecting ducts when aquaporins are inserted.
steps.outcome: Urine concentration and water excretion adjust to protect body-fluid balance.
steps.advanced: Countercurrent multiplication builds the medullary gradient, vasa recta exchange preserves it, and ADH regulates aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting-duct principal cells.
steps.summary: The loop of Henle and collecting duct tune final water conservation and urine concentration.
steps.question: What is a major renal effect of antidiuretic hormone?
options: Hold the aortic valve open longer in systole
steps.feedback: ADH increases aquaporin-2 insertion, allowing more water to leave the collecting duct when a medullary gradient is present.
